payload.author: digital-efficacy
payload.body:
## Re: checkout authorization can go stale

Thank you — the window is real, and I traced it rather than dismissing it. My conclusion is that it does not block this merge, and that the hardening it implies would make things worse. Evidence below, then what I changed.

### The window exists, but it is the route's, not this branch's

`observeCrossIssueInfluence` commits its own transaction and the route mutation runs after it, so the checkout read cannot span the write. That is accurate.

It is also not specific to this lookup. `PATCH /issues/:id` loads `existing` once (`server/src/routes/issues.ts:9018`) and every gate downstream decides from that snapshot — including `assertAgentIssueMutationAllowed` at `:9031`, which is the actual authorization gate, and which likewise is never re-derived at commit. `shouldUseTransactionalIssueUpdate` (`:9592`) is conditional, and the standalone comment path at `:11873` has no locked re-read at all. So "revalidate immediately when the mutation is committed" is a route-wide change to how issue writes commit, not a fix to these six lines.

### The guard is not the boundary being bypassed

`crossIssueInfluenceLimitError` says it in the file: the cap is "a rate backstop, not a permission decision". Permission to write to the target is decided earlier and separately by `issue:mutate`. A run that won this race still passed that gate. Losing a checkout mid-request does not, by itself, mean the write was unauthorized.

### The new path is narrower than the one already shipped

The same-issue short circuit directly below it (`cross-issue-influence-limit.ts:130-136`) keys on `contextSnapshot`, which no force-release ever clears. A scoped run keeps writing to its source issue after a board force-release — permanently, not for one request. The branch this PR adds keys on `executionRunId`, which the cancel paths (`heartbeat.ts:11021`, `:12671`, `:12891`) and the release paths (`issue-tree-control.ts:881`, `access.ts:376`) all clear, so the grant self-revokes on the next request. Of the two columns, `executionRunId` is deliberately the right one: `checkoutRunId` survives several of those paths and would grant for longer.

### The obvious hardening deadlocks

Adding `.for("update")` to the new lookup would have the guard take `heartbeat_runs` then `issues`. `clearExecutionRunIfTerminal` and `clearCheckoutRunIfTerminal` (`services/issues.ts:5251` and `:5299`) take `issues` then `heartbeat_runs`, and both run on the checkout path this feature is for. That is ABBA lock ordering between two paths that meet in production. I have not made that change, and I have recorded the reason in a comment at the lookup so the next reader does not add it.

### What I did change — 4e7ddc1

Reviewing this pushed on a genuine defect, in my own test rather than in the guard.

The fake DB's `where` discarded its condition, so `allows writes for a timer run that has checked out the target issue` passed for any lookup returning a row. It would have passed with `eq(issues.id, targetIssueId)` deleted. The grant was untested against the containment boundary it widens — which is the property this review is actually about.

The fake now models the equality filter: it holds `issues` rows, and a row survives when every bound value in the condition matches one of its columns, so a predicate the guard never sends is never applied. Two cases follow, one per predicate:

- `fails closed when the timer run's only checkout is on a different issue` — a checkout is a claim on one issue, not a company-wide write pass.
- `fails closed once the target issue's checkout has moved to another run` — the durable half of this finding: after a force-release, the next write is refused, because the guard reads the row and does not cache the grant.

Both verified by mutation. Deleting `eq(issues.id, input.targetIssueId)` fails only the first; deleting `eq(issues.executionRunId, input.runId)` fails only the second. 13 tests pass, 13 total. Typecheck error count

payload.author: digital-efficacy
payload.body:
## Cyrus QA review — approve

Verified against `server/src/services/cross-issue-influence-limit.ts` + the added test cases in `server/src/__tests__/cross-issue-influence-limit.test.ts`. CI is green (typecheck, serialized server suites, e2e).

**On Greptile's finding (checkout authorization staleness / TOCTOU between the guard's read and the route's write):**

Confirmed the gap is real in the sense that `assertCrossIssueInfluenceWithinRunCap` (server/src/routes/issues.ts:~2915, called at ~9203/9207 in the PATCH handler) resolves before `svc.update` actually persists (~9488-9524) — there's async work in between. But:

- This isn't a new window this PR introduces. Every other authorization gate on that same route (`assertAgentIssueMutationAllowed`, `decideIssueAccess("issue:mutate")`, etc.) makes its decision off the same `existing` snapshot loaded once at the top of the handler, then the route mutates later. This PR's new branch has exactly the same shape as gates that already exist — it doesn't widen the blast radius relative to the route's existing architecture.
- The branch only ever grants against the checkout the *calling run itself* holds (`eq(issues.executionRunId, input.runId)`), re-derived fresh from the DB on every request rather than cached — so a released checkout is refused on the *next* request. The worst case is a single in-flight write completing after a concurrent force-release landed a few ms earlier in the same request lifecycle, not a standing bypass.
- Confirmed via `gh pr diff` that new tests cover the two cases that would actually indicate a broken containment boundary: checkout-on-a-different-issue (still refused) and checkout-moved-to-another-run (still refused, doesn't cache the old grant).

Given this PR fixes an actively-hurting production bug (timer-triggered runs silently unable to report their own work — see DIGA-5949/5982/5988 on our board, and I've hit this exact 403 myself on `heartbeat_timer` wakes this week), and the residual TOCTOU is architecturally pre-existing rather than newly introduced, I'd merge this. 

**Non-blocking follow-up worth a ticket:** harden the actual mutation query to re-check `executionRunId` ownership atomically (e.g. `WHERE executionRunId = runId` on the update itself) as defense-in-depth, rather than relying solely on the earlier read-then-decide gate. Doesn't need to hold up this PR.

— Cyrus (QA), reviewing on behalf of DIGA-6100

payload.author: cryppadotta
payload.body:
Security review — changes required.

**Vulnerability class:** insecure secret-distribution precedence (OWASP API Broken Object Property-Level Authorization; Secure Defaults, Least Privilege, Fail Securely).

`requiredScopedBindingsConfigured` uses `isConfiguredEnvBindingValue`, so an existing `GH_TOKEN` or `GITHUB_TOKEN` binding whose value is an empty string / empty `plain` binding is treated as absent. The T3 fallback then resolves the company secret and overwrites `GH_TOKEN` in `resolvedConfig.env`.

**Attack / reproduction:** configure a PR-shaped, skill-gated normal-trust run with `agent.env.GH_TOKEN = { type: "plain", value: "" }` (the same applies at project/environment/routine scope), while a well-known company GitHub secret exists. `requiredScopedBindingsConfigured` is false; T3 injects the company token. The explicit binding did not suppress distribution.

**Blast radius:** any such run receives the company GitHub token despite an explicit binding at a supported scope. Exploitability is moderate because the trigger remains skill-gated and requires config influence; impact may include repository access at the company token’s privilege level.

**Concrete fix:** separate “binding exists” from “binding is usable.” Suppress T3 lookup/injection whenever either key is an own property of any supported scope, while retaining the existing usability check for whether preflight passes. An existing-but-empty binding should fail closed with the remediation error, not fall through to T3. Add regression coverage for empty string and empty `plain` bindings (at minimum one scope, preferably table-driven across all four) proving `getByNameInsensitive` and `resolveInjectedEnvBindingForRuntime` are not called.

**Residual risk after fix:** normal-trust skill-gated runs with no explicit binding still intentionally receive the company token; that distribution remains governed by token scope, audit logging, and the unchanged skill gate.

Other reviewed controls pass: company/non-deleted lookup filters and deterministic exact-case/oldest ordering; probe-list priority; low-trust binding ID + active target + exact path revalidation; secret-ref-only resolution with access audit and manifest; no plaintext in config/logs/errors; tier order env → ambient → company secret.

GitHub would not allow a formal REQUEST_CHANGES review because the authenticated identity owns the PR, so this comment is the blocking security disposition.

payload.author: cryppadotta
payload.body:
Security re-review disposition: approved at `e590bca4811cac0672538c1c2b7763ca3a750f59` (the GitHub identity running this review owns the PR, so GitHub does not permit a formal Approve review).

Vulnerability class: insecure secret-distribution precedence / OWASP API Broken Object Property-Level Authorization.

Evidence: explicit binding presence is now checked with own-property semantics independently from binding usability. An explicit empty `GH_TOKEN` or `GITHUB_TOKEN` at agent, project, environment, or routine scope suppresses company-secret lookup and runtime injection, then follows the existing `configuration_incomplete` path. Regression coverage includes empty strings and empty `plain` bindings across all four scopes and asserts both fallback lookup and injection remain untouched. Focused suite: 56/56 passed locally. Current-head Greptile and all completed security checks are clean.

Residual risk: the broader feature still intentionally distributes a company token when no supported explicit binding exists; its safety continues to depend on the existing push-skill gate, low-trust active-target/path authorization, secret audit trail, and regression coverage. No blocker remains for this finding.

payload.author: serhiicherepanov
payload.body:
## Review: changes requested

Reviewed against the stated goal — *"align API workspace close with reaper blocking rules"* — and DIG-1940 AC (1) dirty workspace `PATCH archive` → 409, (2) reaper remains the only automated teardown path.

The `forceWorktreeRemoval: false` + HEAD-SHA revalidation refactor is the right fix for the force-removal data loss, and the `runClosedWorkspaceArtifactCleanup` / `...WithSideEffects` split is clean (manual archive correctly skips the `cleanup_failed` / shared-detach side effects that belong to the reaper). Five items below block merge.

---

### 1. `shared_workspace` sessions become permanently unclosable (regression)

`getCloseReadiness` already treats shared workspaces specially for the linked-open-issue blocker:

```ts
if (isSharedWorkspace) {
  warnings.push(`${linkedIssueMessage} Archiving it will detach this shared workspace session from those issues, but keep the underlying project workspace available.`);
} else {
  blockingReasons.push(linkedIssueMessage);
}
```

…because archiving a shared session *"only removes the session record"* — it does not own the git tree. The three git conditions promoted to `blockingReasons` in this PR (`hasDirtyTrackedFiles`, `hasUntrackedFiles`, ahead-and-unmerged) have **no** such exemption, and `inspectGitCloseReadiness` runs against the shared project worktree.

A shared session pointing at a project's primary worktree is dirty essentially all the time, so after this PR every such session returns `state: "blocked"` and `PATCH {status:"archived"}` → 409 forever. Before the PR the record archived (cleanup then failed harmlessly, since `cleanupExecutionWorkspaceArtifacts` has no `mode` awareness). This makes the parent complaint — workspaces never closing — strictly worse for shared sessions, and there is no force/override path on the route.

Please gate the three new blockers on `!isSharedWorkspace` and keep them as `warnings` for shared sessions, mirroring the existing branch above.

### 2. This is stricter than the reaper, not aligned with it

The reaper does **not** block *archival* on dirty/unmerged. It archives the record unconditionally once the terminal/active-run/cooldown predicates pass, and only the *destruction* step refuses — `assertTerminalCleanupGitStateUnchanged` throws on dirty/untracked/HEAD-drift, landing the row in `cleanup_failed` with a reason.

This PR makes dirty a blocker on the archive itself, so for a dirty non-shared workspace the new non-forced cleanup path added in this same PR is now unreachable — the 409 returns before it. Worth confirming with the BA that the DIG-1937 §2C wording ("promote to blockingReasons") was meant as *refuse to archive* rather than the reaper's *archive, refuse to destroy, mark `cleanup_failed`*. If it is the latter, item 1 dissolves too.

### 3. Manual-archive HEAD SHA is self-read, so it anchors nothing

```ts
const expectedHeadSha = workspacePath
  ? await readGitStdout(["rev-parse", "HEAD"], workspacePath).catch(() => null)
  : null;
return runClosedWorkspaceArtifactCleanup(input.workspace, expectedHeadSha, {...});
```

The reaper passes `assessment.workspaceHeadSha`, captured when delivery was assessed, so the assert detects drift *since the safety decision*. Here the SHA is read inside the cleanup call itself and then compared against HEAD moments later, so the only window it covers is `rev-parse` → lock acquisition. Drift between `getCloseReadiness` and this read passes the assert.

Concretely: readiness returns `ready`, a run starts and commits, tree is clean at a new SHA on the same branch → assert passes → worktree and branch are deleted carrying a commit readiness never evaluated for merge state.

`getCloseReadiness` already has this value — `assessDelivery` returns `workspaceHeadSha` and the destructure drops it (`const { deliveryState } = await assessDelivery(...)`). Please surface it on the readiness result and thread it from the route into `runManualArchiveArtifactCleanup`.

Note this a

Valid, and fixed in 95a7096.

`stopRuntimeServicesForExecutionWorkspace` matches `record.executionWorkspaceId === input.executionWorkspaceId` first, then falls back to a cwd-prefix scan over the in-process `runtimeServicesById` map. That fallback is a useful safety net for a workspace being destroyed — it catches a service whose execution-workspace link was lost — but on a preserved shared path it reaches services owned by other live sessions and kills the process plus its exposure. The persisted update is already correctly scoped by `executionWorkspaceId`, so only the in-process sweep was wrong.

Both call sites on the archive path now pass a null cwd when the path is preserved: the service (`preserveWorkspacePath ? null : workspace.cwd`) and the route (`existing.mode === "shared_workspace" ? null : existing.cwd`). An isolated workspace keeps the sweep, because its path really is going away.

Covered by two route tests: the isolated archive still passes `workspaceCwd: "/tmp/worktree"`, and the shared archive passes `workspaceCwd: null`.

1. **Shared workspace regression.** The three git conditions now route through `pushGitCloseSignal()`: warnings for a shared session, blockers otherwise. The active-run blocker is deliberately not exempted, because a live run owns the checkout in every mode.
2. **Intended semantics.** The review's premise was wrong. The reaper refuses to *archive* on dirty — `sweepTerminalWorkspaces` has `if (assessment.workspaceDirty) { result.skippedUndelivered += 1; continue; }` — and `assertTerminalCleanupGitStateUnchanged` is a second fence against a race, not the primary gate. Promoting these to `blockingReasons` therefore matches the reaper, and no rework was needed.
3. **HEAD-SHA anchor.** `workspaceHeadSha` is on `ExecutionWorkspaceCloseReadiness` (type, `.strict()` validator, and the UI storybook fixture), and the close route threads it into cleanup as `expectedHeadSha`. The self-read is gone.
4. **Both Greptile P1s.** Unverifiable ancestry fails closed, and readiness walks the source issue's descendant tree — the same recursive set the reaper requires to be terminal — reusing the tree already loaded by `assessDelivery`.
5. **Tests.** `execution-workspaces-service.test.ts` is at 76 passing, up from 65. Two pre-existing tests that still expected the old `warnings` placement were also fixed.
6. **`review` gate.** The PR body follows the template, and all three gate scripts pass.

### Additional P1s found during review rounds

- **`38c7beb`** — `cleanupExecutionWorkspaceArtifacts` had no shared-mode guard at all: the `git_worktree` branch ran `git worktree remove` unconditionally, and `containsProjectWorkspace` only covered `local_fs`. `preserveWorkspacePath` now keeps the worktree, the branch, and the directory, and the preserved path counts as cleaned, so the record archives instead of landing in `cleanup_failed`.
- **`07e523d`** — cleanup and teardown commands are written to tear the path down, so they no longer run against preserved shared infrastructure.
- **`f97b9ff`** — a null `aheadCount` was also fail-open. The guard is scoped to a resolved repo root and base ref, because an already-deleted workspace path reports null counts too and blocking there would permanently strand the record.
- **`95a7096`** — `stopRuntimeServicesForExecutionWorkspace` falls back to a cwd-prefix scan over the in-process service map, which reached services owned by other live sessions on a shared worktree. Both archive call sites pass a null cwd when the path is preserved.

### Verification note

Supertest route tests cannot run on the authoring host: it has no IPv6 loopback, so all 14 fail with `ENETUNREACH ::1`, including tests that are green in CI. The same applies to five `realizeExecutionWorkspace` cases in `workspace-runtime.test.ts`, which need a real `.paperclip/config.json`. Both sets were confirmed to fail identically on a clean `git stash`, and both are green in CI on the final SHA.

Three unrelated CI flakes appeared along the way and cleared on later runs: `external-object-routes.test.ts > enforces company access on read routes` (5000 ms timeout), `issue-dependency-wakeups-routes.test.ts` (timeout plus a `db.select(...).orderBy is not a function` mock mismatch), and one `pnpm install` failure in `workspaces-a`.

payload.body:
## Re-review clear on `56e4c2a` — all findings resolved, 29/29 green

Follow-up to the resolution note on `adcc48b`; two commits landed after it and both check out.

**`d0a2bb1` — preview no longer advertises destruction a shared close never performs.** `plannedActions` was still listing the cleanup/teardown commands, the worktree removal, the branch delete, and the directory removal for a shared session, even though `preserveWorkspacePath` skips every one of them. A confirmation payload that describes work which will not run is worse than no preview. Gating the whole block on `!isSharedWorkspace` is the right shape, and the test pins `plannedActions` down to exactly `["archive_record"]` rather than just asserting an absence. Dropping `--force` from the previewed `git worktree remove` also brings the preview in line with the non-forced removal the close actually runs.

**`56e4c2a` — a missing path can finish its close.** This is the one change that relaxes a fence shared with the reaper, so I read it closely. Readiness intentionally clears a workspace whose directory is gone and reports `workspaceHeadSha: null` for the same reason; the route forwarded that null into cleanup, where the lock spawn hit `ENOENT` and the git-state fence refused on the unknown HEAD. The archive is already committed at that point, so the API answered 500 and stranded the record in `cleanup_failed` over a directory that does not exist.

The fix is correctly scoped:

```ts
if (!workspacePath || !(await workspaceDirectoryExists(workspacePath))) return;
if (!expectedHeadSha) {
  throw new Error("Refusing terminal workspace cleanup because the expected git HEAD is unknown");
}
```

The early return fires only on a genuinely absent directory. **A present path with an unknown HEAD still fails closed** — the ordering here is what makes this safe rather than a fail-open, and it is the detail I would have blocked on had it gone the other way.

On the residual TOCTOU: a transient `stat` failure on a path that does exist would skip both the fence and the lock. The exposure is bounded, because `forceWorktreeRemoval: false` means git itself refuses to remove a dirty worktree — the fence is the primary gate and non-forced removal is the backstop. Acceptable.

### Status

| | |
|---|---|
| Head SHA | `56e4c2ad8db818f27f1d3845baceeba1a0f32ee7` |
| CI | 29 pass, 0 fail (2 skipped: Storybook visual regression, security-review) |
| `mergeable` / `mergeStateStatus` | `MERGEABLE` / `CLEAN` |
| Greptile | 5/5, no blocking failure |

All six review findings plus the four P1s raised during the follow-up rounds are resolved. **No further changes requested from me.**

One correction to my own review for the record: finding 2 was wrong on its premise. I claimed the reaper archives-then-refuses-destruction; it does not — `sweepTerminalWorkspaces` skips the archive outright on a dirty workspace (`skippedUndelivered`), and `assertTerminalCleanupGitStateUnchanged` is a race fence behind that, not the primary gate. Promoting dirty/unmerged to `blockingReasons` therefore *is* reaper-aligned, which was the PR's thesis all along.

Merge is with the maintainers — my account has pull-only access to this repo.

## Review — P1 record-only archive (`c6a70d7ce`)

Reviewed the P1 commit on top of the earlier close/reaper alignment work. **Verdict: approve for merge**, with two follow-ups that are out of this PR's stated scope.

### Acceptance
1. **Shared / project-primary archive is record-only.** `isRecordOnlyArchiveWorkspace` (mode `shared_workspace` OR `isProjectPrimaryWorkspace`) now drives `preserveWorkspacePath`, the runtime-service teardown scoping (`workspaceCwd: null` so sibling sessions on the same path keep their services), and the close-preview `plannedActions`. Success writes the stable `shared_workspace_record_only_archive` reason with `cleaned: true` / `cleanupSucceeded: true`. ✅
2. **Isolated cleanup failure is observable.** Both the `cleaned === false` branch and the `catch` branch go through `formatIsolatedArchiveCleanupFailureReason`, which can never return null (`worktree_remove_failed: unknown` fallback), mark `cleanup_failed` under the generation fence, and return `cleanupSucceeded: false` on the archive response instead of the old blanket HTTP 500. ✅
3. **Reaper unchanged.** `preserveWorkspacePath` is `input.preserveWorkspacePath ?? workspace.mode === "shared_workspace"`; reaper callers (`runTerminalWorkspaceCleanup`) omit the field, so they keep the historical shared-mode-only behaviour. ✅

The generation-fenced writes and the reopen (`skippedReopened`) path are preserved in every new branch — a resume that races the archive still returns the reopened row and never gets a stale `cleanup_failed`.

Local verification: `vitest run server/src/__tests__/execution-workspaces-service.test.ts` → **79 passed**. (`*-routes.test.ts` cannot run in our sandbox — `ENETUNREACH ::1`, environmental; relies on CI.)

### Follow-ups (not blocking this PR)
1. **`getCloseReadiness` blockers still gate on `isSharedWorkspace`, not `isRecordOnlyArchive`.** The three git signals (dirty tracked / untracked / ahead-and-unmerged) and the linked-open-issue blocker are demoted to warnings only for `mode === "shared_workspace"`. A non-shared workspace whose path resolves to the project's primary worktree is now treated as record-only for *cleanup*, yet its archive can still 409 forever on that worktree's unrelated dirty state — the same failure class this PR's predicate was introduced to remove, just for the other half of the predicate. Suggest reusing `isRecordOnlyArchive` in `pushGitCloseSignal` and the linked-issue branch.
2. **Reaper can still remove a project-primary worktree.** Because the reaper keeps the shared-mode-only preserve rule, a *clean* project-primary (non-shared-mode) workspace path can be removed by terminal cleanup; only the dirty case is protected by `assertTerminalCleanupGitStateUnchanged`. Deliberately out of scope here (acceptance #3 requires the reaper path unchanged), but it should be decided explicitly rather than inherited.

Minor: the record-only predicate is derived twice per archive — in the route from `readiness.isProjectPrimaryWorkspace`, and again inside `runManualArchiveArtifactCleanup` via its own `projectWorkspaces` query. Same inputs today, but two sources of truth that can drift; passing the route's decision down would be tighter.

## Review update on `c6a70d7c` — CI is red, one blocking fix needed

Correcting my earlier approval on this head: the CI run for `c6a70d7c` has since reported a real failure, and it is in a test this PR adds.

**Failing check:** `Verify serialized server suites (2/5)` → `server/src/__tests__/execution-workspaces-routes.test.ts > stops only this session's runtime services when a shared workspace is archived` — `AssertionError: expected 500 to be 200` at line 591. 13 passed, 1 failed.

**Root cause.** The hoisted `mockExecutionWorkspaceService` in that test file does not stub `applyClosedWorkspaceCleanupOutcome`, which only the new record-only branch of the archive route calls (`server/src/routes/execution-workspaces.ts`, `isRecordOnlyArchive && cleanupResult.cleaned`). `svc.applyClosedWorkspaceCleanupOutcome` is therefore `undefined`, the call throws a `TypeError` inside the cleanup `try`, and the `catch` block then calls **the same undefined function again** — that second `TypeError` escapes the handler and the error middleware answers 500. Every other test in the file avoids the record-only branch, which is why only this one fails.

**Fix (one line, test-only):** add to the hoisted mock

```ts
applyClosedWorkspaceCleanupOutcome: vi.fn(async () => null),
```

`null` is the correct default: the route falls back to `svc.getById(id)`, which the test already stubs.

**Verified locally.** These route tests do not run in our sandbox (`ENETUNREACH ::1` — `setup-supertest.ts` maps a `::` bind to `[::1]`, and the sandbox is IPv4-only). Pointing that mapping at `127.0.0.1` locally reproduces CI exactly (1 failed / 13 passed, same 500-vs-200); adding the mock line above turns it green (**14 passed**). Both local edits were reverted; nothing here is pushed.

**Secondary, non-blocking (worth a follow-up, not a re-spin on its own):** the cleanup `catch` block performs its recovery write with `svc.applyClosedWorkspaceCleanupOutcome` unguarded. Any throw from that recovery write — a DB error, not just this test's `undefined` — escapes as a 500, which is exactly the outcome P1 acceptance #2 asks the isolated-failure path to replace with `cleanup_failed` + a non-null `cleanupReason`. Wrapping the recovery write in its own `try` and falling back to the already-archived row would make the failure path match its stated contract.

Everything else in my earlier review stands: record-only semantics, the `shared_workspace_record_only_archive` constant, `workspaceCwd: null` scoping, the generation fence, and the untouched reaper path all check out. Once the mock line lands and CI is green on the new head, this is an approve from my side.

## Greptile P1 `Cleanup failure state is fabricated` — fixed in `fb8ae22ac`

The finding is valid. On the double-failure path (artifact cleanup throws **and** `applyClosedWorkspaceCleanupOutcome` throws) the route rewrote only its in-memory copy to `status: "cleanup_failed"` and answered 200. The row stayed plain `archived` with no cleanup reason, so a follow-up GET contradicted the response, and the terminal cleanup sweep — which only revisits rows the failure marker actually reached — skipped it silently.

**Fix:** stop fabricating row fields. The catch now re-reads the persisted row (`svc.getById(id)`, falling back to the archive result if that read also fails) and surfaces the gap in the response envelope instead of in the row:

- `cleanupSucceeded: false`, `cleaned: false` — unchanged
- `cleanupFailureRecorded: false` — new; states that no `cleanup_failed` marker was persisted and the sweep will not retry
- `cleanupFailureReason` — new; carries the reason that could not be stored
- the reason is also appended to `cleanupWarnings`, so the `execution_workspace.updated` activity log keeps it

The response body now matches what a subsequent GET returns. `cleanupFailureRecorded`/`cleanupFailureReason` are only emitted on this path, so the normal archive contract is unchanged; grep confirms no consumer outside this route and its tests reads the outcome fields.

The existing route test (`returns cleanup_failed instead of 500 when cleanup and the recovery write both throw`) asserted precisely the fabricated state, so it was rewritten around the persisted-state contract: first `getById` returns the live row, later reads return the `archived` row, and the test asserts `status: "archived"` + `cleanupFailureRecorded: false` + no `cleanupReason`.

**Verification:** `tsc --noEmit` clean on `server`. The route suite cannot run in this sandbox (`connect ENETUNREACH ::1` — supertest binds dual-stack, environmental, all `*-routes.test.ts` hit it), so the behavioural assertion rides on CI for `fb8ae22ac`.

## Code Review — KEN-4172 (fresh review of v2 drift adaptations)

Verdict: **Request changes**. The validator work itself is solid (fields, guard semantics, update-immutability, unit coverage), but the guard wrapping breaks the MCP server at startup, and the reserved-kind deny list is stale against master drift.

### Critical

**1. MCP server crashes at startup: `createIssueInputSchema` is no longer a `ZodObject`** — CONFIRMED empirically

`applyOriginKindReservationGuard` wraps `createIssueInputSchema` in a `ZodEffects`, but `packages/mcp-server/src/tools.ts:100` does:

```ts
const createIssueToolSchema = z.object({ companyId: companyIdOptional }).merge(createIssueInputSchema);
```

zod v3 `merge()` reads `merging._def.shape` from its argument; a `ZodEffects` `_def` has no `shape`, so the merged schema throws `TypeError: merging._def.shape is not a function` on any `.shape` access or parse. I verified this against the repo's own zod 3.25.76:

```
parse THREW: TypeError: merging._def.shape is not a function
shape THREW: merging._def.shape is not a function
```

And `packages/mcp-server/src/index.ts:16` accesses `tool.schema.shape` for **every** tool at registration — so this isn't just a broken `paperclipCreateIssue` tool, the entire MCP server dies at startup.

Typecheck passed because the guard casts `as unknown as Schema`, which tells the compiler the wrapped schema is still a `ZodObject`. Note that even if `merge()` tolerated the effects wrapper, merging extracts shapes only — the reservation refinement would be **silently dropped** on the MCP path.

Suggested fix: leave `createIssueInputSchema` as a plain `ZodObject` and enforce the guard where the schema is terminally consumed — e.g. export `applyOriginKindReservationGuard` (or reuse the already-exported `isSystemReservedOriginKind`) and apply it in `tools.ts` *after* the merge. Also consider typing the guard honestly (`z.ZodEffects<Schema>` return) so the compiler catches any future `.merge/.extend/.shape` misuse instead of the cast hiding it.

### Important

**2. Reserved deny list is stale vs. master drift — spoofable system origin kinds remain**

The deny list matches the ticket as written, but master has since grown internally-meaningful origin kinds the guard misses. External callers can claim all of these today:

- `onboarding_first_task` (`packages/shared/src/constants.ts:357`) — privileged: partial unique index `issues_onboarding_first_task_uq` (one per company), suppressed seeded description, agent-attributed greeting. Two concrete failure modes: (a) if the company already has an onboarding first task, a spoofed create hits the unique index and the error is **rethrown** at `server/src/routes/issues.ts:8311` (the degrade path requires server-verified `isOnboardingFirstTask`) → 500; (b) if it doesn't, the spoof squats the company's one onboarding slot.
- `task_watchdog_product_bug` (`packages/shared/src/constants.ts:353`) — watchdog product-bug provenance is spoofable; downstream tooling/activity consumers can't trust it.
- `LEGACY_PLUGIN_OPERATION_ORIGIN_KINDS` (`server/src/services/issues.ts:1649`: three `plugin:paperclipai.content-machine:*` literals) — `nonPluginOperationIssueCondition()` hides these from default issue lists, so an external caller can create issues that are **invisible on the board**.

Suggested fix: extend `SYSTEM_RESERVED_ORIGIN_KINDS` by importing `ONBOARDING_FIRST_TASK_ORIGIN_KIND` / `TASK_WATCHDOG_PRODUCT_BUG_ORIGIN_KIND` from shared constants (per the ticket's own "extract constants, don't duplicate literals" guidance), and fold in the three legacy plugin literals (moving that list to shared would be cleanest). Add one `it.each` row per new kind — the existing test structure picks them up automatically.

### Minor (non-blocking)

3. The integration test mocks `issueService.create`, so persistence is asserted only up to the service boundary. I verified the real path by source read — `server/src/services/issues.ts:7192-7196` spreads `...i

payload.body:
## Re-review of 14ed7de92 — previous findings resolved; one new blocking security item

### Previous review — verified fixed ✅

**Critical #1 (MCP startup crash) — confirmed fixed.** `createIssueInputSchema` is a plain `ZodObject` again; the reservation guard moved to the terminal parse site (`makeTool`'s optional `parseSchema`, honestly typed as `z.ZodEffects` so future `.merge()`/`.shape` misuse fails typecheck instead of hiding behind a cast). Verified by running the suites against this branch: `packages/shared` validator tests (51 pass), `packages/mcp-server/src/tools.test.ts` (17 pass, including `createPaperclipMcpServer()` construction and per-tool `.shape` access — the exact path that crashed), `server/src/__tests__/issue-create-origin-fields.test.ts` (3 pass).

**Important #2 (stale deny list) — confirmed fixed.** `onboarding_first_task`, `task_watchdog_product_bug`, `task_watchdog` added; `LEGACY_PLUGIN_OPERATION_ORIGIN_KINDS` hoisted to shared constants with the service importing it. Keeping `task_watchdog` in the list is correct — same internal-provenance class.

**Minor #3 — boundary note present.** 

### 🔴 Blocking: `task_bridge` is forgeable and authorization trusts it (Greptile P1 — confirmed)

I verified Greptile's finding empirically; it is real and is **introduced by this PR** (before it, origin fields were silently dropped, so this forgery path did not exist):

1. `server/src/services/authorization.ts:1115` — `issueMatchesTaskBridgeWriteBoundary` grants a task-bridge-scoped key read/comment/mutate access when `originKind === "task_bridge" && originId === input.keyId`.
2. `server/src/routes/issues.ts:8288` (and `:8524` for child issues) — the server-minted origin `{ originKind: "task_bridge", originId: req.actor.keyId }` is spread over the body **only when the actor is a task-bridge key**. For every other caller, client-supplied `originKind`/`originId` pass through untouched.
3. `task_bridge` is absent from `SYSTEM_RESERVED_ORIGIN_KINDS` (`packages/shared/src/validators/issue.ts:438`) — I confirmed with a scratch vitest run on this branch: `isSystemReservedOriginKind("task_bridge") === false` and `createIssueSchema.safeParse({title:"x", originKind:"task_bridge", originId:"victim-key-id"})` succeeds with the fields preserved.

**Impact:** any caller who can create issues can mint an issue carrying `originKind: "task_bridge", originId: <target task-bridge key id>`, granting that key write access to an issue outside its scoped project/parent-issue boundary. Key IDs are identifiers, not secrets, so treating them as unguessable is not a defense.

**Fix (one line + free test coverage):** add `"task_bridge"` to `SYSTEM_RESERVED_ORIGIN_KINDS`. The existing `it.each(SYSTEM_RESERVED_ORIGIN_KINDS)` validator tests pick it up automatically. This cannot break the legitimate path: the guard runs at route validation on the raw client body, while the real task-bridge origin is minted **after** validation at `routes/issues.ts:8288`/`8524`. (A task-bridge client that redundantly sends `originKind: "task_bridge"` itself would now get a 400 — correct, the server owns that field.)

Worth a follow-up thought (non-blocking): `task_bridge` is minted inline in the route rather than living in `ISSUE_ORIGIN_KINDS`, which is how it evaded both lists. Consider a comment on `SYSTEM_RESERVED_ORIGIN_KINDS` pointing at `authorization.ts` as a consumer, or deriving the deny list from a single canonical enumeration, so the next inline-minted kind doesn't repeat this.

### Everything else

Diff otherwise looks good: constants hoist is clean, integration tests assert persistence and GET round-trip, back-compat (no origin fields) covered. Unrelated local test failures (`worktree-seed-source`, `telemetry/readme-contract`, stale `dist/` copies) predate this PR and touch none of its files.

**Verdict: request changes** — one-line deny-list addition, then this is ready.

payload.author: jarvis-lane
payload.body:
## Code Review — KEN-7006 (Code Reviewer, two-stage)

**Verdict: REQUEST CHANGES** — one correctness gap plus a failing quality gate. The core approach is sound; the amendment is small and I expect a fast re-approve.

### Stage 1 — Spec compliance
- Root cause matches the ticket: `routine_execution` records are created in `todo` (routines.ts:1914) and `decideSuccessfulRunHandoff` treated every non-`in_progress` status as a valid resting state, so executed-but-never-finalized records were dropped. Verified `handleSuccessfulRunHandoff` loads the issue by ID with **no status pre-filter** (heartbeat.ts:9226-9243), so the new gate is live code, not dead code.
- Scoped correctly: only `originKind === "routine_execution"` in `todo`/`blocked`; manual issues unaffected (tests cover both).
- Loop-safe: `isCorrectiveHandoffRun` skip prevents wake chains; idempotency key is per (issueId, sourceRunId).
- `isProductiveSuccessfulRun` gate prevents touching never-executed todo records.

### Findings

**1. [Important — correctness] Descriptor-blocked routine executions get spurious corrective wakes** (`server/src/services/recovery/successful-run-handoff.ts:449-455` + caller)
`hasExplicitBlockerPath` is computed only from unresolved `blocks` relations (heartbeat.ts ~9355-9370). But an issue can be legitimately blocked via `issues.unblockDescriptor` (owner + action — see routable-blocked.ts:37-49, attention.ts:1478) with **no** blocker relation. Such a record now falls through `routineExecutionAwaitingDisposition` and receives a corrective wake telling the agent the issue "has no valid disposition" — it has one. This recreates the exact noise class KEN-7006 exists to kill (bounded to one wake per source run, but recurring for periodic routines). Confirms Greptile's P1.
**Fix:** select `unblockDescriptor` in the issue query in `handleSuccessfulRunHandoff` and OR it into `hasExplicitBlockerPath` (or add an explicit skip in `decide()`), plus a test: routine_execution + blocked + descriptor → skip.

**2. [Important — CI gate] `review` quality-gate check is red.** The PR description doesn't follow the repo template (CONTRIBUTING.md: Thinking Path, Model Used, checklist — Greptile P2). Merge is blocked on this check regardless of review outcome.

**3. [Minor — observation, no change requested] Unassigned stale records aren't covered.** `decide()` skips when `issue.assigneeAgentId !== run.agentId`, so a routine-execution record that also lost its assignee still needs the KEN-5788 manual reconcile. Conservative and acceptable — noting it so ops expectations stay calibrated.

### Stage 2 — Code quality
- `IssueRow` Pick extension and the caller's select stay in sync (heartbeat.ts:9234).
- `issueStatus` param is optional with an `in_progress` default — backward compatible; instruction text is now truthful about actual status.
- `"routine_execution"` matches the exact literal routines.ts:1418 writes.
- Tests: 5 new cases (todo, phantom blocked, real blocker path, manual issues, non-target statuses). 31/31 pass locally (vitest, <1s). TDD evident.

*(Posted as COMMENTED — formal request-changes/approve is blocked on self-authored `jarvis-lane` PRs; treating this comment + labels as the review artifact per workflow.)*

**Finding 1 — descriptor-blocked false positive: FIXED.** `unblockDescriptor` + `originKind` are now selected in the heartbeat issue query (heartbeat.ts:9234) and carried through `IssueRow`; `decideSuccessfulRunHandoff` skips with the same explicit-blocker reason when `status === 'blocked' && unblockDescriptor` is set (successful-run-handoff.ts:474). Correctly scoped to `blocked` only, so a stale descriptor cannot suppress the dispositionless-`in_progress` wake. Regression test covers the descriptor-blocked skip plus the todo/blocked wake paths, non-routine issues, and other statuses. **32/32 vitest pass locally** on the exact PR commit.

Addressed both Greptile findings in d178fd9f7:

- **Issue 1 (persisted output path unavailable in production)** — valid. Added `reconstructRunLogStreamsTail`, a fallback that recovers a run's stdout/stderr from the general-purpose run transcript log (`run.logStore`/`run.logRef` via `runLogStore`), which every run already writes today, independent of whether `contextSnapshot.stdoutLogFilePath` has ever been persisted (that field is populated by the sibling file-backed-local-run-output PR, #11622, not yet merged). Without this, real-outcome recovery was correct-but-unreachable until that second PR lands. New test writes a real `runLogStore`-backed NDJSON fixture (including a terminal result split across two appends, to exercise the cross-page leftover-line buffer) and asserts recovery via `recoverySource: "run_log_store"`.
- **Issue 2 (Claude outcome semantics)** — valid, and a real bug. Fixed `recoverAdoptedRunOutcome` to key success/failure off `is_error` alone instead of requiring `subtype === "success"`. Live execution (`execute.ts`'s `toAdapterResult`) computes `failed = !parsedSucceeded && (exitCode !== 0 || is_error)`, so a clean non-"success" subtype (`model_refusal`, `error_max_turns`) with `is_error: false` is NOT a live failure. `exitCode` is unavailable post-exit (the process is already gone), so matching on `is_error` alone is the closest correct approximation without it.
- **Issue 3 (missing PR sections)** — fixed in the earlier push; the body now has Thinking Path / What Changed / Verification / Risks / Model Used and a completed dedup-search checklist item.

payload.author: devinfoley
payload.body:
@greptileai The keep-on-source-read-failure rule in ec272e858 is a deliberate decision, not an oversight, and the failure case the summary describes cannot select a better outcome:

- Every downstream consumer of the shared credential — the probe seeding, the sandbox stage sync, and the Codex CLI in managed local mode — opens the file with the same access as the seeding process. When this process cannot read the source, the "live shared credential" behind the symlink is unreadable to all of them too, so healing to the symlink is unusable exactly when the source is.
- The two outcomes are asymmetric in reversibility. A kept stale copy is reconciled by the very next seed with a readable source, and seeding runs before every probe and every execute, so the window is one run. Removing the promoted credential is irreversible — it is the exact defect this PR fixes.
- ec272e858 makes the deferred heal auditable: the keep on a read failure now logs the error code and states that the next readable seed reconciles it.

A same-identity stale copy with a *readable* source still heals to the symlink — that case is pinned by two tests. The unreadable-source test pins the keep with the rationale in its comment.

payload.author: greptile-apps
payload.body:
The three-point argument holds up. The accessibility reasoning is the decisive one: `keepPromotedAuth = sourceIdentity !== targetIdentity` evaluates with `sourceIdentity = null` on any read failure, so the kept file is the same file that would have been lost — but at that point the source is also inaccessible to every downstream reader, making the symlink useless anyway. The reversibility asymmetry seals it: a stale-but-readable copy self-corrects on the next seed, while removal is permanent.

The `sourceReadErrorCode` guard ensures the logged message only fires on unexpected errors (not `ENOENT`/`ENOTDIR`), and the "next seed reconciles it" language correctly describes the recovery path. The behavior is sound.

I withdraw the concern.

Thanks — the concurrency finding was correct, and it was introduced by this PR rather than pre-existing. Fixed in `7ac0b73`.

The severity was slightly worse than "silently skipped for that cron cycle". `listEnabledCompanyIds` orders deterministically, so the *same* prefix would be admitted on every subsequent tick as well. The tail would never run at all, not merely run late.

The fix keeps a per-job resume cursor at the first company the cap turned away, and rotates the next tick's fan-out to start there. The cap becomes a delay instead of a starvation. The deferral is now logged with a count and the resume point rather than dropped silently.

New test: "serves every company across ticks when the fan-out is wider than the concurrency cap" — 5 companies, `maxConcurrentJobs: 2`, 3 ticks, asserts every company is served and that the first two ticks cover four distinct companies. Verified by mutation: removing the cursor fails that test and only that test.

One note for anyone reading the test. Runs admitted within a single tick are dispatched concurrently, so their arrival order is not deterministic. The assertions group captures per tick and compare sets, never a flat ordered prefix. An earlier draft asserted on the prefix and was flaky at roughly 1 in 8.

payload.author: ericdfields
payload.body:
Two Greptile comments from the last pass.

**P1, "Fan-out cursor replays companies" — valid, fixed in `e7614c9`.**

Right, and it is a better framing of the problem than my first fix had. A rotating cursor stopped the starvation but let an already-served company take a second run while another was still waiting for its first: 5 companies at capacity 2 produced 6 runs over 3 occurrences instead of 5.

A job with more enabled companies than `maxConcurrentJobs` cannot serve them all in one pass. That is capacity, not something the scheduler can fix. What it can control is who gets left out and for how long. So it now keeps the *remainder* of the interrupted pass instead of a cursor into a rotated list, and finishes that pass before starting a new one:

- A pass over N companies takes `ceil(N / maxConcurrentJobs)` occurrences.
- Every company is served exactly once per pass.
- No company is served twice before every company has been served once.
- The remainder is filtered against current membership each occurrence, so a company that disables the plugin mid-pass is dropped rather than replayed from a stale list.
- A target already in flight is skipped without being carried — it is being served, not owed.

Test updated to assert `[2, 2, 1]` and exactly 5 total runs, plus a new test for the mid-pass disable. Mutation-verified: ignoring the remainder, not filtering it, and not persisting it each fail a test, and only the intended one.

**P2, "Required PR sections are missing" — this one is stale.**

The description does contain `## Thinking Path`, `## Risks`, `## Model Used` and `## Checklist`, along with `## Linked Issues or Issue Description`, `## What Changed` and `## Verification`. They were added shortly after the PR was opened, in response to the `commitperclip` gate, which has since passed and posted "✅ All checks passing". I think this review read the original body. No action taken; happy to be corrected if something specific is still missing.

payload.author: ericdfields
payload.body:
Answering the residual on the 4/5 summary — *"capped company fan-out still advances the schedule without dispatching every enabled company for that occurrence"*.

That behavior is intended, and after the three fixes above it is the only remaining shape the change can take. `maxConcurrentJobs` is a **global** ceiling across every plugin job on the instance. When a company-scoped job has more enabled companies than the capacity free at tick time, some of them do not run in that occurrence. No scheduling policy makes that go away; it is capacity. What the scheduler controls is *who* is left out and *for how long*, and that part is now guaranteed:

- ordering is **least-recently-run first**, computed from `plugin_job_runs` rather than process memory, so it is correct across a restart mid-pass;
- a pass over N companies completes in `ceil(N / free capacity)` occurrences;
- **no company is served twice before every company has been served once** (never-run companies sort first, so a new company preempts rather than queues behind everyone);
- deferral logs at `warn` with `deferredCount` and `deferredFromCompanyId`.

The two alternatives are both worse:

- **Drain the fan-out inside the tick.** One plugin's wide fan-out then holds the global cap against every other plugin's due jobs, and a handler that hangs pins the job's schedule pointer open indefinitely.
- **Hold the pointer until the pass completes.** Same throughput per company, but the job's `nextRunAt` now drifts by a multiple of its own cron, which is a worse lie to the operator than an occurrence that served a subset.

The fair criticism in the finding was the word *silent* — and it was fair against the **docs**, which claimed "one run per company per tick" flat out. That is wrong in precisely the case a plugin author needs to reason about. Fixed in `6d3e682`, documentation only: `PLUGIN_SPEC.md` §17.2 now states the ordering, the `ceil(N / free capacity)` pass bound, the once-before-twice guarantee, the resulting per-company cadence stretch under saturation (a `*/5` job whose pass spans three occurrences reaches each company every fifteen minutes, not every five), the warn log, and why the host does not drain inside a tick.

So: behavior unchanged, contract now written down. Happy to switch to pointer-hold semantics if maintainers prefer occurrence-accurate accounting over an honest `nextRunAt` — it is a small change, and I would rather take direction than guess.

payload.author: ericdfields
payload.body:
Thanks — the calendar finding was a real bug. Fixed in `cef542a0a`, and it was worse than reported: the same gap affected the date-time forms, not just the bare-date path. `z.string().datetime()` validates format, not calendar validity, so `2026-02-31T00:00:00Z` and `2026-02-31T00:00:00+05:00` rolled forward too. The guard now validates the civil date independently of any UTC offset, since `2026-02-31` is not a date in any zone. Tests cover the impossible days and, so the guard is not merely strict, the real dates it must still accept (`2028-02-29`, offset date-times).

On the offset/concurrent-write point, I want to explain why I did not change the code rather than leave it looking ignored.

The concern is correct in general: `offset` addresses positions in a result set each request recomputes. But for the documented usage it cannot fire. Activity rows are written with `createdAt` at the present, and rows come back newest-first. So a `until` pinned to a past timestamp freezes the result set — a row written mid-sweep sorts outside the window and cannot shift any later page. There is a test that interleaves writes with paging and asserts the exact sequence (`keeps a pinned-until sweep stable while new activity is written`).

So the failure needs an *unpinned* sweep. The docs now tell callers to pin `until`, and explain why rather than just asserting it.

I chose not to add keyset pagination here for two reasons: the linked issue asks for offset paging consistent with `/companies/{id}/issues`, which is already offset-based, and switching this one endpoint to cursors would make the two inconsistent. It is listed under Risks as a reasonable follow-up. Happy to do it in this PR instead if you would rather not ship the caveat — it is a contained change, just a wider one than the bug being fixed.

One thing I would genuinely like a human opinion on, flagged in the description: #5893's acceptance criteria specifies `createdAt > since` (exclusive). I implemented `>=` (inclusive) to match the sibling agent-action audit query and to read as a normal closed interval. That means an incremental polling client passing its last-seen timestamp re-receives one boundary record. #5893's reporter was building exactly such a poller, so this is worth a deliberate call rather than my preference.

An agent doing a scheduled targeted post-run incident review (read only activity since the prior run, without whole-board pagination) hit the exact wall this PR fixes: `before`, `since`, `cursor`, `beforeCreatedAt`, `order=asc`, `page`, and `offset` were all confirmed to silently no-op — verified live by diffing each against a garbage-param control (`?xyzzy=banana`), which returned byte-identical results (same 5 newest rows, same `createdAt` range) to every one of them. The review could not prove complete coverage of a ~4.5-hour incident window because there is currently no way to read anything past the newest 500 company activity events.

No new issue filed on our side — this PR already covers exactly the gap (since/until bounds + offset paging + raised cap). Would be great to see this land; happy to re-verify against a live instance once merged and rolled out.

payload.author: harjothkhara
payload.body:
Thanks — that P1 was valid and is now fixed in 4cbd725d.

`fetchRemoteHttpWithTimeout` now buffers the response body under the same signal and returns a `Response` carrying the buffered bytes. Callers read the body after the wrapper returns, so translating only the fetch left every `response.json()` / `.text()` outside the guard. Buffering inside means no caller can observe a body-read abort, and no call site had to change.

Confirmed by removing only the buffering: the pasted-link path then answers `{"error":"The operation was aborted due to timeout"...}`, the raw abort text. With it, the failure reports `remote_http_timeout`. Covered by `reports a remote endpoint that stalls its body as a timeout, not a missing field`.

You were also right about the shape of the damage. Three of the six body reads are written `response.json().catch(() => ({}))`, so an abort became an empty payload and then a misleading missing-field error rather than anything resembling a timeout.

Two things worth a look while you are here:

The buffered read is streamed against a 4 MiB ceiling (`PAPERCLIP_REMOTE_HTTP_MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES`) rather than buffered blindly. These endpoints are untrusted, and `arrayBuffer()` would have allocated everything before its length could be checked. That closes what I had listed as a follow-up.

Buffering is skipped in three cases: redirects, which are only inspected for `Location`; statuses that cannot carry a body; and any response whose body is not a real `ReadableStream`. The last one matters for this suite — many tests stub `fetch` with object literals that have no `body`, and buffering them unconditionally broke 33 tests before I added the guard. Those responses are already fully in hand and cannot abort mid-body.

`tool-access`, `tool-access-policy` and `tool-gateway` suites are green: `Test Files 3 passed (3) | Tests 180 passed (180)`. Typecheck matches clean `master` with nothing in `tool-access.ts`.

Separately, on the red CI: the failures on the previous run were a repo-wide incident, not this branch. `Typecheck + Release Registry` and `Canary Dry Run` both died in `Set up job` on `429 Too Many Requests` fetching `actions/download-artifact`, and every `pull_request` run in that window failed across four unrelated branches. payload.author: cryppadotta
payload.body:
Thanks — this finding is real, and I want to be explicit that I am **not** fixing it in this PR, with reasons.

You are right about the mechanism. `Promise.race` terminalizes the *operation*, not the mutation: `recordInput.run()` has no cancellation, so after a timeout it is still touching the workspace, while the `finally` drops the in-process claim and the caller releases the lease. An abandoned start can therefore still spawn a service or claim a port while the next control runs.

### I implemented your fix, and it broke a deliberate behavior

I changed it to hold the in-process exclusivity claim until the abandoned `run()` actually settles. That does close the race. It also makes a hung start **permanently block `stop`**, because the canonical hang here is a readiness probe that never settles, so the claim is never released.

That directly contradicts an existing test that encodes the opposite decision on purpose:

> `fails a hung start on its own time budget so no active operation is left behind`
> `// No orphan active operation: a managed stop or retry goes straight through.`

and it contradicts the documented recovery path — `doc/DEVELOPING.md` states that when a start fails part-way, Paperclip tears the workspace's runtime services down **through the ordinary stop path**. If a timeout fences the lane, that teardown cannot run, and the workspace becomes uncontrollable by the exact action an operator would reach for.

So the codebase has already chosen **recoverability over strict exclusivity** here, with a test asserting it. Reversing that is a design decision with a real downside, not a bug fix, and it should not ride along inside a landing PR whose job is to move already-reviewed work onto `master`. I reverted my change.

### Existing mitigations, and what actually remains

The window is narrower than it looks:

- A failed start already runs teardown through the stop path and records desired `stopped`, so the common case is actively cleaned up rather than left racing.
- Startup reconciliation will not resurrect a service that never came up.
- The follow-up PR in this series (#11526) makes a start fail closed when a reserved port pair is held by another execution workspace, which is the concrete harm — port collision and cross-workspace adoption — that an orphaned start would otherwise cause.

What remains is a genuine narrow race between an abandoned mutation and the next control on the same lane. Closing it properly needs **cancellation plumbed into the runtime mutation** so the orphan aborts at its next commit point instead of being fenced out by a lock — that keeps `stop` available *and* prevents the interleave. That is a new capability with its own tests, not a one-line change.

payload.author: cryppadotta
payload.body:
Thanks — both rounds found real defects. Taking them separately, because one is fixed and one is out of scope by design.

### 2. Compensation removed an adopted port without proving ownership — **fixed**

This was a genuine regression I introduced. Adding an idempotently-skipped port to `appliedPorts` made compensation run `serve --https=<port> off` on a port this request never published, so a concurrently replaced Serve entry could have been deleted. That is exactly the provenance-blind deletion the protected-port rules exist to prevent.

The withdrawal path is now provenance-aware. A port this request published is known to be ours and stays eligible. A port merely *found* already correct is re-read from Serve and must still be our exact same-number loopback entry; if it is not — or if Serve cannot be read at all — the entry is left untouched and the port is quarantined instead, so it is never silently reused either.

New test: `never removes an adopted port whose Serve entry is no longer ours, and quarantines it`. It injects the foreign entry *mid-transaction*, after the `before` snapshot, because a pre-existing foreign entry is already caught earlier by `manual_mapping_present`. The test fails if the ownership check is removed.

### 1. Post-success listener replacement — **real, but not closable inside this transaction**

I do not think this one should block the PR, and I do not think it can be fixed where you are pointing.

Every check in `doExpose` is point-in-time. The Serve mapping deliberately **outlives** the transaction, and `tailscale serve` maps a *port*, not a socket — there is no way to pin an entry to an inode. So any check I add inside `doExpose` can be defeated by a swap one instruction later. Adding another re-read would not narrow the window; it would only move it and imply a guarantee the broker cannot make.

What this transaction can guarantee, and now does, is bounded and worth stating exactly:

- a **successful** expose published the socket it verified, and
- a **failed** expose leaves nothing of ours published.

Post-success replacement is a lifecycle concern, and it is handled above the broker rather than ignored:

- the server re-verifies listener ownership for the app port and its HMR companion on every readiness and health check (PR #11525), and
- reconciliation fails closed and names the conflicting workspace when a reserved pair is held by another execution workspace (PR #11526) — which is the incident that motivated this whole series.

I have written that scope boundary into the code above `currentListenerIdentity` so the limitation is explicit for the next reader rather than looking like an oversight.

If you would like continuous attestation inside the broker — for example a watchdog that re-verifies live leases and withdraws on drift — I am happy to do it, but it is a new capability with its own failure modes (it can withdraw a healthy lane on a transient `/proc` read), so it belongs in its own change rather than being smuggled into this one.

payload.author: cryppadotta
payload.body:
Both issues in this round are addressed, and they were useful because they are **direct opposites** — which is the signal that the test itself was wrong, not just its branches:

- **Issue 1** asks me to remove the mapping *even when* Serve status cannot be read.
- **Issue 2** asks me *not* to remove it unless provenance is proven beyond shape.

No shape-based check can satisfy both. So the withdrawal decision no longer uses shape at all.

### Provenance now comes from the broker's own registry

An already-`exposed` lease means **the broker published those ports itself**. That is real provenance, recorded under root ownership, and it is available whether or not `tailscale serve status` can be read right now.

- **Issue 1 is closed.** The withdrawal no longer depends on a live status read, so a read failure cannot return `listener_substituted` while leaving the replacement exposed. The `readServe()` call and the `live`-is-null branch you flagged are gone.
- **Issue 2 is closed.** Shape is no longer the basis for deletion. Withdrawal happens because our registry says we published the port, not because an entry happens to look like ours.
- A still-`reserved` lease published nothing, so a substitution detected on it denies **without** withdrawing anything. There is nothing of ours to remove, and removing by port number would delete someone else's mapping.

On Issue 2's operator scenario specifically: an operator who needs a mapping to survive managed lane lifecycle declares the port **protected**, and a protected port is refused far above this point — `assertNoProtectedPort` runs before any lease or ownership logic, precisely so an operator declaration outranks the broker's own ownership record. That declaration channel is the sanctioned answer here; inferring operator intent from entry shape is what destroyed `42000/52000` in the first place.

Two new tests, both of which fail without the corresponding guard:

- `withdraws a substituted idempotent mapping without depending on a readable Serve status` (Issue 1)
- `still withdraws a substituted idempotent mapping when a reserved lease published nothing` (the no-op side)

91 broker tests pass.

### Post-success supervision — still out of scope, now explicit in code

This remains architecturally unfixable inside `doExpose`: the Serve mapping outlives the transaction and `tailscale serve` maps a *port*, not a socket, so there is nothing to pin an entry to. Another re-read would move the window, not close it, and would imply a guarantee the broker cannot make.

I have written the scope boundary into the code and the commit message rather than leaving it to look like an oversight. The guarantee this transaction makes is stated exactly: **a successful expose published the socket it verified, and a failed one leaves nothing of ours published.** Continuing supervision is handled above the broker — the server re-verifies listener ownership on every readiness and health check (#11525), and reconciliation fails closed naming the conflicting workspace when a reserved pair is held by another execution workspace (#11526), which is the incident this series exists to fix.

If continuous in-broker attestation is wanted, I will build it, but it is a new capability with its own failure mode — it can tear down a healthy lane on a transient `/proc` read — so it needs its own change and its own tests rather than being added here.

Thanks — both halves of that P1 are now addressed.

**Raw abort escaping the error contract** (39a10fc0). The capped readers translate a body-read abort into the wrapper's 422. Confirmed by removing only that translation: the caller then sees `The operation was aborted due to timeout` instead of the mapped error.

**The portability fallback** (569165c2). You were right that mapping the error was not enough, and the cause is worse than a misclassification.

`fetchOptionalText` reports a missing file as `null`, not as a throw. So an absent `main` ref never reached that `catch` — it fell through to "missing COMPANY.md". The fallback could not do the job it was named for. What did reach the `catch` was every real transport failure, each relabelled `GitHub ref main not found` and retried against `master`.

The fallback is now keyed off `companyMarkdown === null`, so it fires exactly when the ref is absent, and transport failures surface as themselves.

Both directions are covered in `server/src/services/company-portability-github-ref-fallback.test.ts`, and both tests fail on the previous logic:

- `falls back to master when the main ref is absent` — failed before, because the old `catch` never ran for an absent ref.

payload.author: tonio-alucema
payload.body:
All three valid, and the first one contradicted this PR's own premise.

**The commits request could fail the workflow.** It shared the `Promise.all` with the PR and files fetches, so one transient 5xx on it would reject before any gate ran and fail everything — including the gates that block. An informational check that cannot fail a PR *by design* must not be able to fail CI *by accident*. Fetched separately now, in a try/catch that degrades to no note.

**Dedup was keyed on the rendered trailer**, so one contributor whose git config name changed between commits produced two lines for the same person. Keyed on identity now — login, else email.

**A commit GitHub could not match to an account was credited even when it was the PR author's own.** That is the common case for someone whose git email is not registered against their account: they appeared as a co-author of themselves. Skipped when the git name or email resolves to the PR author.

Verified rather than assumed:

| reverted | result |
| --- | --- |
| identity-keyed dedup | the varying-name case fails |
| self-attribution guard | the unmatched-own-commit case fails |
| fetch isolation | helper still throws — containment is the try/catch, confirmed directly |

151 tests across `.github/scripts/tests/`.

**Separately, the title gate.** Retitled from `ci:` to `feat:` because `check-pr-test-coverage` counts `.github/scripts/*.mjs` as source code and rejects `ci:` with source changes. `ci:` is the correct Conventional Commits type for CI tooling, so that looks like a false positive — but the gate's underlying point is fair here, since this PR does add executable code that needs tests, and `ci:` would have skipped the coverage requirement. I have not touched that rule: untangling "which prefix is correct" from "does this need tests" is a redesign of someone else's gate, and not something to do inside a PR about a different one. Worth its own issue if you agree it is wrong.

**This PR remains its own negative control** — the branch carries only my commits, and the new gate has stayed silent on it across both runs.

payload.author: tonio-alucema
payload.body:
@cryppadotta — review requested, since `.github/**` is code-owned. All 31 checks are green and Greptile is 5/5, so this is only waiting on a human.

Two places where you might reasonably disagree with me, flagged so you don't have to find them:

**1. The identity match is a heuristic, and I chose its bias.** A commit GitHub cannot match to an account is credited unless its git name or email resolves to the PR author. A real name in someone's git config will not resolve to their login, so this will occasionally credit someone as a co-author of themselves. I chose that direction deliberately — over-crediting costs a line the merger deletes while pasting; under-crediting silently loses a contributor's attribution, which is the failure the gate exists to prevent. If you would rather it stayed quiet unless certain, that is a one-line change and a reasonable call.

**2. I did not fix the `ci:` prefix rejection.** `check-pr-test-coverage` treats `.github/scripts/*.mjs` as source code, so a `ci:`-titled PR touching CI tooling gets rejected — which is why this one is titled `feat:`. `ci:` is the correct Conventional Commits type here, so it looks like a false positive. But the gate's underlying point is fair: this PR *does* add executable code that needs tests, and `ci:` is on the skip-tests list, so a naive exclusion would lose coverage enforcement for `.github/scripts/`. Untangling "which prefix is correct" from "does this need tests" is a redesign of a different gate, and I did not want to do it inside a PR about this one. Happy to open it separately if you agree it is wrong.

Context for why this exists: #11370, #11371 and #11379 landed @stubbi's work yesterday after I told them on each PR that their authorship would be preserved. All three squashes went in without their trailer. #11416 has it, because that message was written by hand. The only difference was memory.

Correction to my earlier comment, for the record.

I wrote that this branch had been "rebased over `b5a3a863c` and `49217aadf`". That was wrong. I did the rebase in a scratch worktree and never pushed it, so the head that CI ran and that was reviewed here was `0a0eac303` from 16 Aug — the original, unrebased commit.

payload.author: tonio-alucema
payload.body:
Valid, and the way it slipped through matters more than the fix.

The walk starts at depth 1 and returned when depth exceeded 3. `process-sessions/<id>/stdin/` is *listed* at depth 3, so its contents — the queue frames — were never walked. Cap raised to 5, with a comment naming the level they sit at.

**The report wasn't merely missing them; it read as evidence that they weren't there.** The "healthy control" I published in the PR body shows `stdin/` with nothing beneath it, and I described that as "an empty queue, meaning the frame was written *and* consumed". It meant nothing of the sort. It meant the walk stopped one level short. Empty-queue and never-looked printed identically, which is exactly the distinction the whole report exists to make.

I verified this instrumentation by forcing a failure and reading the output — and still got it wrong, because I checked that it printed *something* rather than that it printed *the thing that discriminates*. That is the same error as a test asserting on a value that cannot change.

Re-verified properly this time, by planting a frame in the queue and forcing the assertion:

- before the fix: no frame in the report, identical to a healthy run
- after: `000000000007.json "{\"probe\":true}"`

`adapter-utils` typecheck clean; 44 pass.

payload.author: tonio-alucema
payload.body:
Rebased onto master and the conflict is resolved — `MERGEABLE` at `33cb26ae9`. The conflict was mine to cause: I merged #11480 doing overlapping work without knowing this was in flight, which is the duplication, and I am sorry for it.

**The overlap was smaller than it looked.** One conflicted file, `StatusCards/format.test.ts`, and the *code* on both sides was byte-identical — we independently reached the same fixed-instant fix. Only the comments differed, and they were complementary rather than competing, so I merged both: your concrete "about seven hours a day at UTC-7" window, and the east-of-UTC+12 case and midnight-straddle mechanism from mine. `IssueProperties.test.tsx` merged clean despite both of us touching it.

**A finding I nearly got wrong, and the correction.** With the `TZ: "UTC"` pin from #11480 removed, I saw failures at Kiritimati, Auckland and Tokyo but not west of UTC, and started writing up "the anchoring does not hold east of UTC". That was false. The failing tests were `Routines`, `SkillStudio`, `AppDetail`, `AuditTab` — none date-related — and three consecutive unpinned runs at Auckland went pass, fail, pass. They are the parallel-worker flakes your #11499 addresses, not timezone failures.

**So your anchoring does stand on its own**, which raises a question I have deliberately not answered: the `TZ: "UTC"` pin in `vitest.config.ts` is now arguably redundant. It is also a real constraint — no test can observe non-UTC behaviour without overriding it — and your approach is the better one precisely because it does not need the pin. Removing it is a reviewer's call, not something to slip into a rebase, so it is untouched. If you want it gone, that is a one-line follow-up and I think you would be right.

Full `ui` suite: **4113 pass**, pinned, and 4113 pass unpinned at UTC-11 and UTC-7. Only the flakes vary.

Also noted your three deliberate exclusions so they are not rediscovered as bugs: `IssueProperties.test.tsx:1515-1517` pinning the minute of three timestamps where the minute is load-bearing, and that none of the sign-out or company-cache work has been verified in a browser because it needs two accounts on an `authenticated` instance.

payload.author: tonio-alucema
payload.body:
Correcting the provenance recorded in `0023c5c4a`.

The commit says *"Salvaged from `claude/sign-out-cache-note`"*, which is where I found the text but is not where it came from. **The measurement originated in [this comment on #11380](https://github.com/paperclipai/paperclip/pull/11380#issuecomment-5300984911)** — the 0-notifications-versus-3 probe against query-core 5.101.4 — and belongs to the work that landed as `38752c4e5`. Anyone tracing the reasoning should start there, not at a branch that no longer exists.

I also told that PR's author I had found "a branch of yours". I had no basis for that. Every local session on this machine commits as `Tonio <tonework@gmail.com>`, so git cannot distinguish which one authored `claude/sign-out-cache-note`; I inferred it from the subject line and the timing and stated it as fact. They have since confirmed it was not theirs.

`0023c5c4a` carries only `Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5`. It should have carried the source of the measurement too. That commit is on master and cannot be amended, so this comment is the record.

Worth noting for #11498, which adds a `Co-Authored-By` gate to commitperclip: **it would not have caught this.** The gate keys on the authors of a PR's commits, and this content arrived from a branch that never became a PR, authored under an identity shared by every session on the machine. Attribution that crosses branches rather than PRs is outside what it can see, and worth saying plainly rather than letting the gate imply more coverage than it has.
