payload.author: nickyleach
payload.body:
Blocking merge-readiness feedback for the public capability contract:

The original nested-over-legacy API mismatch in this comment was fixed on `83bd3bd`. The remaining documentation and concurrency findings below are merge-blocking, not optional follow-ups.

### [Blocking] Document the complete public contract

This PR adds seven public manifest fields but no plugin documentation describes them. The PR checklist also says documentation was updated. Code comments and tests are not sufficient documentation for plugin authors.

**Required documentation:** update `doc/plugins/PLUGIN_SPEC.md` or the canonical sandbox-provider contract and cover all of the following:

- The seven supported keys: `reusableLeases`, `nativeSyncIn`, `nativeSyncOut`, `concurrentSyncAndExec`, `concurrentSyncOperations`, `persistentProcessSessions`, and `independentControlCommands`.
- The declaration is optional and partial. For a valid, identified provider, an omitted key defers to verified worker discovery; `false` narrows support; `true` never grants support without verified prerequisites.
- Nested `sandboxCapabilities.reusableLeases` overrides legacy `supportsReusableLeases` when both exist.
- The worker-method prerequisites for every capability, including both lifecycle methods required for reusable leases.
- Target/config narrowing and failure behavior: ephemeral lease policy, job/native-sync restrictions, `useSessions`, config-resolution failure, and exact-plugin identity failure.
- The actual concurrency behavior chosen in the next section. Documentation must not describe either concurrency flag as enforced unless production code enforces it.

**Acceptance:** a third-party provider author can determine exactly what to declare, which worker methods must be advertised, what omission means, and when the host will narrow or deny each capability without reading server source.

### [Blocking] Do not ship no-op concurrency capabilities

`concurrentSyncAndExec` and `concurrentSyncOperations` are currently validated, resolved, serialized, and tested only as data. No production scheduling or synchronization path reads either flag. A provider can declare `false` with no behavioral effect. That makes the public contract misleading and leaves dead capability code in the release.

Choose one complete outcome for this PR:

1. **Enforce them:** identify every production point that can overlap sync with execution or inbound sync with outbound sync, and gate that overlap on the effective snapshot. A denied capability must serialize the relevant operations. Add deterministic tests using deferred promises/barriers that prove operations do not overlap when `false` and preserve allowed overlap when `true`.
2. **Remove them:** if the runtime does not currently expose those concurrency choices, remove both keys from the public type, strict validator, capability key list, prerequisite mapping, effective snapshot, parser, and tests. They can be reintroduced when an enforcing consumer exists.

Document whichever outcome is implemented. Labeling the fields reserved or descriptive is not sufficient for this PR.

These two sections are fixed acceptance criteria. Together with the current inline P1 and P2 comments, they define the complete blocking scope for the next review.

payload.author: YukiCrisp
payload.body:
Greptile P1 addressed in f847d0638.

The finding is right: `sampleBlockerIdentifier` is produced by `classifyPath`, which can forward a sample from further down the chain, while `sampleBlockerEdgeKind` was read off the root's top-level edge. For `root --blocked_by--> A --child--> B` the API reported B as `blocked_by` even though B is not in `blockedBy` — exactly the contradiction this PR exists to remove.

Fix: `classifyPath` now takes the kind of the edge it was reached through and returns it beside the sample. When it forwards a downstream sample it forwards that node's kind with it. The root falls back to its own top-level edge kind only in the case where the sample itself falls back to the top-level node.

The counts stay top-level by definition, so `sampleBlockerEdgeKind` can legitimately disagree with `dependencyBlockerCount` / `childBlockerCount` when the sample is a leaf. That is now stated in the type doc rather than left implicit.

Added `labels a sampled descendant with its own edge kind, not the top-level one` as a regression test for the exact chain in the finding. It fails without the fix. `issue-blocker-attention.test.ts` is 27 tests, 27 passed; root `pnpm typecheck` green.

payload.author: YukiCrisp
payload.body:
Independent inspection (reviewer, not the author). **Verdict: content PASS.** One naming nit, non-blocking.

### Reproduced

- `pnpm --filter @paperclipai/shared build` → clean.
- `vitest run src/__tests__/issue-blocker-attention.test.ts src/__tests__/issues-service.test.ts src/__tests__/attention-service.test.ts` → **169 passed**, Node 22.
- `issue-blocker-attention.test.ts` alone, verbose: **27 passed** = the 24 pre-existing tests unmodified + the 3 new ones. That is the load-bearing evidence for "state / reason / existing counts unchanged", and it holds.
- All CI gates green on `f847d0638`.

(Minor: the description says 196 for the three-file run; I measure 169. Same three files, all green — just noting the number so it is not carried forward.)

### Targeted counter-proof of the Greptile P1 fix

Reverting the whole service file only proves the new fields are absent, which is uninteresting. Instead I reverted **only the edge-kind threading**, keeping every other line of the PR:

```diff
-const classified = downstream.map((edge) => classifyPath(edge.blockerIssueId, nextSeen, edge.kind));
+const classified = downstream.map((edge) => classifyPath(edge.blockerIssueId, nextSeen, edgeKind));
```

```
× labels a sampled descendant with its own edge kind, not the top-level one
- Expected  "sampleBlockerEdgeKind": "child"
+ Received  "sampleBlockerEdgeKind": "blocked_by"
```

That reproduces the reported P1 exactly (`root --blocked_by--> A --child--> B` reporting `B` as `blocked_by`) and shows the regression test is pinned to the one line that fixes it, not to the feature as a whole.

### `appendBlockerAttentionEdges` does not perturb sample selection

Old behaviour: first-seen edge is pushed, later duplicates skipped. New behaviour: first-seen edge is pushed, later duplicates `continue` after possibly upgrading `kind`. Array contents and insertion order are identical in both, so `topLevelEdges` ordering — and therefore `classified[0]`, `sampleEntry`, and the fallback sample — is unchanged. The `blocked_by` upgrade is order-independent as the comment claims, and the mutated objects come from fresh `.map(...)` results, so nothing aliases back into the query rows.

The `firstDownstream` extraction is likewise behaviour-preserving for `sampleBlockerIdentifier`: `classified[0]?.sampleBlockerIdentifier ?? nodeSample` and `firstDownstream?.sampleBlockerIdentifier ?? nodeSample` agree on every input, since `firstDownstream` is null exactly when `classified[0]`'s sample is falsy.

### On "the sample kind need not agree with the top-level counts"

Documenting it on the type is the right call and, given no consumer renders the field yet, proportionate. Two things make it stick better than a comment alone: the counts are a strict partition (`dependencyBlockerCount + childBlockerCount === unresolvedBlockerCount`, including the both-child-and-dependency case, which dedup collapses to a single `blocked_by` edge — covered by the `PBF` test), and the descendant case has its own regression test.

**Nit, non-blocking:** `sampleBlockerEdgeKind` parses most naturally as "the kind of the sampled *top-level blocker's* edge", which is precisely the reading the doc comment then has to walk back. `sampleBlockerIncomingEdgeKind` would carry the semantics in the name and leave the doc as background rather than as a correction. Not worth a rev on its own.

Independent inspection (reviewer, not the author). **Verdict: content PASS.** Notes below are evidence and two non-blocking observations.

### Reproduced

- `pnpm --filter @paperclipai/server exec vitest run src/__tests__/routines-service.test.ts` → **65 passed**, Node 22.
- All CI gates green on `465608a2b` (build, typecheck, 5 server shards, 5 serialized shards, 3 e2e shards, policy, review, Greptile, Socket, Snyk).

### Counter-proof that the new coverage is pinned to the change

Restoring only `server/src/services/routines.ts` to `master` and keeping the new tests:

```
× keeps a delegating routine run in flight while the execution issue waits on a covered blocker
  Tests  1 failed | 64 skipped (65)
```

So the first test genuinely fails without the fix; it is not vacuous.

### The premise the fix rests on holds

The change is only safe if a `blocked` issue with no live blocker cannot classify as `covered`. It cannot — `listIssueBlockerAttentionMap` short-circuits before classification:

```ts
// server/src/services/issues.ts:2749
if (topLevelEdges.length === 0) {
  attentionMap.set(root.id, createIssueBlockerAttention({
    state: "needs_attention", reason: "attention_required", terminalBlockerIssueId: root.id,
  }));
  continue;
}
```

A `blocked` issue whose blockers are all `done`, or which has no blockers at all, still settles the run as `failed`. That is the case worth protecting and it is protected.

The `attention === null` fallback is also conservative: if `listBlockerAttention` returns no entry for the issue, `blockedExecutionFailureReason(null)` yields the old `"Execution issue moved to blocked"` and the run still fails.

### Three collateral checks

1. **Input shape.** The widened `select` in `syncRunStatusForIssue` matches `IssueBlockerAttentionInputNode` field-for-field (`id`, `companyId`, `parentId`, `identifier`, `title`, `status`, `assigneeAgentId`, `assigneeUserId`, `executionRunId`). No implicit `undefined` reaching the classifier.
2. **No dispatch regression from longer-lived runs.** Concurrency is keyed on `findLiveExecutionIssue` (issue-level) in `dispatchRoutineRun`, not on run status, so a run that stays `issue_created` for the delegation window does not skip or coalesce later scheduled fires.
3. **No consumer parses `failureReason`.** The one place that interpolates it (`services/pipelines.ts:3008`) reads a run immediately after dispatch, guarded by `!run.linkedIssueId`, so it cannot reach the new blocked-branch message. The richer strings are display-only.

### Observation 1 — Risk 2 is real and has no run-level safety net (non-blocking)

The PR body is right that a covered wait that later stalls is never re-evaluated, because nothing calls `syncRunStatusForIssue` outside the two issue-status paths. Worth adding: `routine_runs` has **no staleness sweep either** — outside `services/routines.ts`, the table is only read for `responsibleUserId`/`routineRevisionId` and deleted on company teardown. So such a run stays `issue_created` indefinitely with nothing to reap it.

That is still a better trade than the status quo (a 100% false-positive failure on every delegating routine, which is what motivated this), and the stall remains visible on the blocked-issue attention surface. But it converts a guaranteed false positive into a possible silent false negative at the run level, so it deserves a follow-up rather than being left implicit — either re-sync on blocker-graph transitions, or a periodic sweep over non-terminal `routine_runs`.

### Observation 2 — the #9689 overlap is one line, not a duplicate (non-blocking)

#9689 keeps the "blocked means failed" classification and adds recovery afterwards; this PR changes the classification. They are complementary, and they are genuinely additive in one direction: #9689 restores a stale `failed` run to `issue_created` on resume, which this PR does not do — after this change a run that failed while uncovered and later becomes covered stays `failed` until the issu

payload.author: ericdfields
payload.body:
Thanks — the P1 is real and I have fixed it in 1575d62.

`writeFile`'s `mode` option applies only when it creates the file. On the repair path the managed `config.toml` already exists, and a home seeded by the *previous* copy-the-host-file behaviour inherited the host's mode — often `0644`. So repairing one of those homes rewrote the content and left the managed MCP `Authorization: Bearer` header group- and world-readable. That is precisely the population this PR's repair pass exists to touch, so the finding lands on the highest-risk path.

Added `await fs.chmod(target, 0o600)` after the write, matching the existing pattern in `writeManagedCodexMcpConfig` and `stageCodexHomeEntry`.

Added a regression test that seeds an existing managed config at `0644` and asserts the repair leaves it `0600`. My earlier mode test only covered the *create* path, which is why this slipped through. Mutation-checked: removing the `chmod` fails the new test.

payload.author: ericdfields
payload.body:
Self-review after the mode fix turned up two more defensive gaps in the same function, pushed as `b1a7977`:

- **Same-home guard compared resolved strings.** `$CODEX_HOME` and `~/.codex` can be symlinks, so a managed target that aliases the host home would slip past `path.resolve(a) === path.resolve(b)` and the seed would write over the user's own config — the one thing this function must never do. Now compares real paths, falling back to the resolved string when a path does not exist yet (the managed home usually does not, and in that case it cannot be the host home either).
- **A non-regular file at the managed config path was read through and written over.** A directory or a user-placed symlink there is not Paperclip-written state. It is now left alone, matching the policy `ensureSymlink` already applies to a directory in a managed home. This also removes an `EISDIR` throw that the previous copy-if-absent seeding never raised.

Both are mutation-checked: reverting either guard fails the new tests. 477 tests pass across `packages/adapters/codex-local`, `codex-config-seed`, `acpx-engine/execute` and `codex-local-execute`.

payload.author: dzianisv
payload.body:
Flagging a conflict I found while working on #11421, before this merges.

This PR maps `github-copilot` to `subscription`. The server normalizes that to `subscription_included`:

```ts
// server/src/services/heartbeat.ts
case "subscription":
case "subscription_included":
  return "subscription_included";
...
function normalizeBilledCostCents(costUsd, billingType) {
  if (billingType === "subscription_included") return 0;
```

So every Copilot cost event would be recorded at **0 cents**. On a deployment that routes agents through Copilot, that is the single largest cash lane in the ledger, and it would silently read as free.

Copilot Business is a seat subscription, but the agent traffic on top of it is **not** included usage — it is metered against premium credits and invoiced as overage. Reconciled against a real org bill, that lane was billing roughly $0.0092 per 1,000 tokens with no cache-read discount, which is why #11421 prices it from token counts and stamps `credits`.

Suggested resolution, either order of merge:

- Change `PI_SUBSCRIPTION_PROVIDERS` here so `github-copilot` resolves to `credits`, not `subscription`. `credits` is not zeroed by `normalizeBilledCostCents` and is the accurate description of premium-credit metering.
- On merge with #11421, keep `applyTokenRateCard` wrapping `resolvePiBillingType`. The rate card intentionally wins for billers that have an entry, so the biller-level billing type stays authoritative and the provider heuristic supplies the rest.

The rest of the provider classification in this PR looks right to me and is worth keeping — the `unknown` default for custom providers especially.

payload.author: dzianisv
payload.body:
Both pieces of feedback addressed in `19fce88`.

**@dzianisv — Copilot is `credits`, not `subscription`.** You are right, and the zeroing is the part that makes it dangerous rather than merely imprecise: `subscription` → `subscription_included` → `normalizeBilledCostCents()` returns 0, so the lane reads free instead of reading low. `PI_SUBSCRIPTION_PROVIDERS` is gone; `github-copilot` now sits in `PI_CREDIT_PROVIDERS` next to `openrouter`, with a comment explaining that the seat is a subscription but the agent traffic on top of it is metered premium credits. That composes with #11421 the way you described — the rate card stays authoritative for billers that have an entry, and this heuristic only fills in the rest.

Concrete stakes on the deployment that found this: 518 Copilot cost events over ~36h carrying 82,888 cents of reported cost. Under the old mapping every one of those becomes `$0.00`.

**@greptile-apps — auth-file API runs are no longer classified as subscriptions.** Valid P1, and the honest fix was to stop guessing. The adapter now reads `~/.pi/agent/auth.json` and uses only the `type` discriminator pi stores per provider:

- `api_key` → `api`
- `oauth` → `subscription`
- environment key present → `api` (unchanged, checked first)
- credential not visible → `unknown`

That last branch is the behavioural change: a dual-auth provider (`anthropic`, `openai`, `xai`, `radius`) with no environment key and no readable auth file is now `unknown` instead of `subscription`. `unknown` is not zeroed by the server, so an unobservable credential can never silently erase a real metered bill. This is deliberately stricter than the `claude-local`/`gemini-local` convention, because pi's credential can live in a file the adapter cannot see, whereas `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` is claude-local's only key path.

The auth file lives on the machine that runs pi, so the read is skipped entirely for remote execution targets. It is failure-tolerant (missing/malformed/non-object → empty map, never fatal) and it never reads back, logs or returns secret material — the unit test asserts that the returned map contains no key material.

Verification:

```
$ node_modules/.bin/vitest run packages/adapters/pi-local
 Test Files  5 passed (5)
      Tests  49 passed (49)
$ tsc --noEmit -p packages/adapters/pi-local/tsconfig.json    # clean
```

Against a real host auth file (`{github-copilot: oauth, anthropic: oauth, google: api_key}`):

```
github-copilot -> credits
anthropic      -> subscription
google         -> api
openai         -> unknown      (no credential anywhere)
```

payload.author: greptile-apps
payload.body:
Both P1s resolved cleanly.

**Copilot → `credits`**: The `PI_CREDIT_PROVIDERS` placement is correct and the comment in the set declaration does the right job of explaining the seat/overage distinction for future reviewers. The 82,888-cent stake makes the `subscription`-zeroing risk concrete — good to have that documented.

**Auth file credential kind**: The implementation is exactly right. A few things worth calling out that are done well:

- The remote guard in `execute.ts` (`executionTargetIsRemote ? {} : await readPiAuthCredentialKinds(...)`) is the right place for it — `resolvePiBillingType` stays pure and the caller owns the skip logic.
- `readPiAuthCredentialKinds` correctly strips everything except `type` — the test asserting `JSON.stringify(kinds)` contains no `"secret"` is a good belt-and-suspenders check.
- Falling back to `unknown` instead of `subscription` for an unobservable dual-auth credential is the right conservative choice. The asymmetry with `claude-local`/`gemini-local` is justified by pi's auth-file path.

The `PI_API_KEY_PROVIDERS` set covering `google` correctly means that `GEMINI_API_KEY` in the environment doesn't change the answer — `api` unconditionally — which matches the "this provider has no OAuth path" invariant.

No further concerns on this PR. LGTM.

Tip: You can customize Greptile's behavior for this repo with [`.greptile/rules.md` and `.greptile/config.json`](https://www.greptile.com/docs/code-review/custom-standards).

payload.author: tonio-alucema
payload.body:
Known follow-up, recorded here so it is not lost.

The post-sign-in path in this PR uses `cancelQueries` plus `fetchQuery({ staleTime: 0 })`, which guarantees the membership check reads a *query cache* entry fetched for the account that just signed in. It does not guarantee a fresh *HTTP request*. `api.get` coalesces identical in-flight GETs keyed on the request path alone (`coalescedGet` in `ui/src/api/client.ts`), and `companiesListQueryOptions`' query function passes no abort signal, so `cancelQueries` cannot abort the underlying request. A `/companies` request still in flight from before the sign-in can therefore answer the forced fetch.

The exposure is narrower than it sounds, and the common case fails safe: a request issued while signed out answers 401, which the query function folds to `{ companies: [], unauthorized: true }`. An empty list is never read as membership. What remains is the case where a request was issued under a *previous account's* session and is still in flight when the new sign-in completes.

#11430 adds `detachInflightGet(path)` and `companiesApi.detachInflightList()` for this. Rather than land the same helper in two PRs, this one picks it up by rebasing on whichever of #11430 / #11380 merges first.

payload.author: tonio-alucema
payload.body:
Valid — fixed, and the way I first tested it is worth recording.

**The finding.** `hydratedMissionForRef` is a ref, so it outlives the state it describes. `reset()` clears `companyGoal` on close, the marker stayed set, and the next run for the same company skipped hydration while the hire proceeded — the original defect back again by another route. The marker now travels with the field it describes: cleared in `clearCompanyScopedState` and in `reset()`, wherever `companyGoal` is cleared.

**My first test for it was worthless.** It passed against the unfixed code. Its close-button lookup matched nothing, optional chaining swallowed the click, so no `reset()` ever ran and the field was never cleared — the test walked a path that had no bug in it. It now asserts the button was found and that the wizard actually left the agent step before reopening.

**And one honest caveat on the fix.** The new case fails only when *both* clears are removed:

| removed | result |
| --- | --- |
| `reset()` clear | passes |
| `clearCompanyScopedState` clear | passes |
| both | fails |

`reset()` also clears `createdCompanyId`, so the next company introduction routes through `clearCompanyScopedState` and clears the marker there anyway. Each is redundant with the other *today*. I kept both deliberately — as one invariant rather than one guard plus a coincidence, since a later `reset()` that preserved the company would silently restore this bug — but I'd rather say that than let the table above look like two independently verified guards.

`ui` typecheck clean; 50 pass across the wizard, mission and hook suites.

payload.author: dzianisv
payload.body:
Reviewed against the AGE-260 design (AGE-250 investigation). Diff matches the spec:

- `TRANSIENT_INFRA_ERROR_RE` covers OAuth refresh / DNS-TCP-reset / socket-hangup families, checked after `CONFIGURATION_INCOMPLETE_ERROR_RE` and `PROVIDER_QUOTA_ERROR_RE` so a dead credential still wins over a network-shaped false positive — confirmed by the `configuration_incomplete`-wins and `provider_quota`-wins regression tests.
- Backoff ladder: 2m/4m/8m/15m/15m/15m, 6 scheduled retries, then falls back to `blocked` + `transient_infra_exhausted` recovery action as backstop. Matches the acceptance criteria's capped-retry requirement.
- Monitor path reuses `scheduleAdapterFailureRecoveryMonitor` for both provider_quota and transient_infra — issue stays in_progress/in_review, `executionPolicy.monitor.nextCheckAt` set, no `escalateStrandedAssignedIssue` call while retries remain.
- Word-boundary fix (`\b(?:502|503|504)\b`) on the bare-status regex is correct and better than Greptile's suggested snippet — the suggested version substring-matches `5024ms` and `1502`, which this PR's version does not (verified with the added regression tests).

Sign-off on the flagged deviation: approved, ship it.

Enabling auto-merge (squash) so this lands once CI is green — no further action needed from me.

Heads-up from a production incident: the provider-quota **monitor** path this PR copies (`scheduleProviderQuotaRecoveryMonitor`) overwrites any already-armed issue monitor.

Please do not extend that slot. Quota recovery is moving onto a dedicated heartbeat `scheduled_retry` in https://github.com/paperclipai/paperclip/pull/12149. Transient infra retries should use that same heartbeat retry lane, not `applyIssueMonitorPolicyTransition`.

payload.author: dzianisv
payload.body:
## Each half of the regression suite fails on its own without the fix

A reviewer on a running deployment (`@paperclipai/server 2026.814.0-canary.7`) reported that the two halves of this bug do **not** behave identically there:

- `PATCH /api/issues/{id} {"assigneeAgentId": ...}` on issues held by a terminated agent returned **200**, not 403.
- `PATCH /api/routines/{id} {"assigneeAgentId": ...}` on a routine held by the same terminated agent still returned **403 `Agents can only manage routines assigned to themselves`**.

Their concern was fair: a suite that terminates an agent and then only proves the *issue* is reclaimable could pass on such a build while the routine stays frozen forever. So I re-verified the suite by reverting only the source changes and keeping the tests.

```
$ git checkout <base> -- server/src/routes/issues.ts server/src/routes/routines.ts \
    server/src/services/authorization.ts server/src/services/issues.ts
$ cd server && npx vitest run src/__tests__/terminated-assignee-reclaim.test.ts

 ❯ src/__tests__/terminated-assignee-reclaim.test.ts (5 tests | 3 failed)
   × lets another agent check out an issue whose assignee was terminated
   × lets another agent mutate an in_progress issue left behind by a terminated assignee
   × lets another agent take over a routine owned by a terminated agent

 Tests  3 failed | 2 passed (5)
```

Failure detail, unmodified:

- checkout → `409 {"error":"Issue checkout conflict","details":{...,"checkoutRunId":null,"executionRunId":null}}`
- issue PATCH → `409 issue_write_assignee_run_lock` — "Terminated VP of Engineering has this task checked out and a run is live"
- routine PATCH → `403 {"error":"Agents can only manage routines assigned to themselves"}`

With the fix restored:

```
$ npx vitest run src/__tests__/terminated-assignee-reclaim.test.ts
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  5 passed (5)
```

Three things worth recording from this:

1. **The routine assertion stands alone.** `lets another agent take over a routine owned by a terminated agent` and `still refuses routine management when the assignee is alive` are separate cases against `PATCH /api/routines/{id}`, covering both `status` and `assigneeAgentId`. Neither depends on the issue boundary, and the first one fails without the `routes/routines.ts` change even when the issue cases are removed. That matches the deployed build: `dist/routes/routines.js` still holds the flat self-ownership check at both call sites, with no terminated-assignee escape and no governance-mode branch.
2. **The issue half can be masked by governance mode.** In a company running the simple governance path, an issue write by a company member is allowed by `allow_simple_company_member`, which is why the reviewer saw 200 on the issue PATCH. The surviving blocker in that configuration is not the boundary but the assignee run lock and the checkout conflict — and both still fail without this PR, as the run above shows. The 403 boundary from the original report is the stricter-governance shape of the same hole; the PR closes all three.
3. **The routine hole is unconditional.** No governance mode, permission grant, or manager relationship gets past that guard today; only a board actor does. That is what leaves a routine owned by a dead agent minting issues nobody can pick up.

No code change from this comment — the suite already asserts the routine path independently, and now there is direct evidence that it fails on its own.

payload.author: dzianisv
payload.body:
Both Greptile P1s were valid. Fixed in b7b6d8b.

**1. Recovery required a heartbeat that a paused agent never gets.** Correct — pausing removed the only path that could observe recovery. Recovery no longer depends on a run:

- Changing the agent's configured instructions path (`adapterConfig.instructionsFilePath`) clears the failure state and lifts the pause, but only when Paperclip applied that pause (`pauseReason: "system"`). This is the "operator corrected the path" case.
- `agentService.resume()` now also drops the failure state, so a resumed agent gets a fresh two-strike window instead of being paused again by its very next run. This is the "operator restored the file" case.
- A later run that reads the file still clears the state, as before.
- The text in `agents.errorReason` now names both actions instead of implying it recovers on its own.

New tests: `lifts the pause without a run when the operator corrects the instructions path` and `gives a resumed agent a fresh grace window`.

**2. Concurrent completions could corrupt health state.** Correct — it was an unlocked read-modify-write on `agents.metadata`. `applyInstructionsReadHealth` now runs inside a transaction and takes `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on the agent row, then evaluates from the locked snapshot. The caller in `heartbeat.ts` passes an `agentId` instead of a pre-read row, so no stale snapshot can reach the write.

New test: `counts concurrent run completions once each instead of losing one` runs two completions with `Promise.all` against embedded Postgres and asserts `consecutiveFailures: 2` plus a paused agent.

Also added: the service refuses to pause a `terminated` or `pending_approval` agent, and `clearInstructionsReadHealth` leaves a manual pause in place.

Verification:

```
npx vitest run server/src/__tests__/agent-instructions-health.test.ts
# Test Files  1 passed (1)
# Tests  17 passed (17)

pnpm --filter @paperclipai/server typecheck   # clean
```

payload.author: dzianisv
payload.body:
Third P1 (resume overwrites newer health state) was valid too. Fixed in fc602d0.

`applyInstructionsReadHealth` locks the agent row, but `agentService.resume` did not — it computed the cleared metadata from the snapshot it read before the write, so a resume that started first could commit stale `agents.metadata` over a failure recorded in the meantime.

`resume` now runs in a transaction and takes `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on the agent row before computing the cleared metadata, so the two writers serialize on the same lock. The transaction is entered with the same `transaction`-capability check `updateAgent` already uses, so a caller holding a tx-bound `db` still works.

New test `does not overwrite a concurrent health write when an operator resumes`: a concurrent writer takes the row lock and stores a marker in `agents.metadata`, the resume is started while that lock is held, then the writer commits. The resume must preserve the marker.

Red/green, against embedded Postgres:

```
# with the fix
npx vitest run server/src/__tests__/agent-instructions-health.test.ts
# Test Files  1 passed (1)
# Tests  18 passed (18)

# with resume reverted to the unlocked version
# AssertionError: expected undefined to be 'run-3'
# Tests  1 failed | 17 passed (18)

pnpm --filter @paperclipai/server typecheck   # exit 0
```

payload.author: dzianisv
payload.body:
Re-raised P1 (`resume` erases newer health state when the run completion wins the lock) is fixed in 868f0fb.

The lock made the two writers serialize but did not decide what should happen when the failure commits first. Resume was still deleting a failure the operator never saw, undoing its pause.

`resume` now compares the health state it read before taking the lock with the state it sees under the lock:

- **Unchanged** — the operator saw everything there is to see, so the state is cleared and the agent gets a full fresh window, as before.
- **Changed** — a failure landed in between. It is rewritten as strike one of the fresh window (`consecutiveFailures: 1`, `pausedAt: null`, `errorReason` kept) instead of being deleted.

So the operator's resume still wins — the agent is never left paused with no way back, which was the first P1 in this review — but the newer failure is not lost: a still-broken instructions path pauses the agent again on the very next run rather than the one after it.

New test `keeps a failure that lands after the operator asked to resume as strike one`: a concurrent writer holds the agent row lock and commits the pausing second failure while the resume is waiting on that lock; the agent must come back `idle` with `consecutiveFailures: 1` and `lastRunId: "run-2"`, and must pause again on the next failed read.

```
npx vitest run server/src/__tests__/agent-instructions-health.test.ts
# Test Files  1 passed (1)
# Tests  19 passed (19)

npx vitest run server/src/__tests__/agents-service-clear-error.test.ts \
  server/src/__tests__/budgets-service.test.ts \
  server/src/__tests__/agent-instructions-service.test.ts
# Test Files  3 passed (3)
# Tests  18 passed (18)

pnpm --filter @paperclipai/server typecheck   # exit 0
```

payload.author: dzianisv
payload.body:
P1 "old runs restore cleared health" was valid. Fixed in 305eee6.

Correcting the path cleared the state, but a run that started before the correction still read the old file and its completion re-created that state — two of them re-paused a freshly corrected agent for a path it no longer uses.

The failure now carries the configured path it came from (`AdapterInstructionsReadFailure.configuredPath`, populated centrally in `readAdapterInstructionsFile`, so every adapter gets it). `evaluateInstructionsReadHealth` compares it with the agent's current `adapterConfig.instructionsFilePath` read under the same row lock, and drops failures from a path the agent no longer uses. `configuredPath` is optional: a failure without it still counts, so an adapter built against the older contract degrades to the previous behaviour instead of going silent again — which is the bug this PR exists to fix.

New tests (all three fail without the guard):

- `ignores a failure reported by a run that used a superseded instructions path`
- `still counts failures from adapters that do not report the configured path`
- `does not re-pause a corrected agent from runs still using the old path` — embedded Postgres: record a failure, correct the path, land two stale completions, assert the agent stays idle with no health state, then assert a failure on the *new* path counts as strike one.

```
npx vitest run server/src/__tests__/agent-instructions-health.test.ts \
  packages/adapter-utils/src/agent-instructions-file.test.ts
# Test Files  2 passed (2)
# Tests  28 passed (28)

# with the guard removed
# Tests  2 failed | 20 passed (22)

pnpm --filter @paperclipai/server typecheck        # exit 0
pnpm --filter @paperclipai/adapter-utils typecheck # exit 0
```

payload.author: dzianisv
payload.body:
P1 "resume overwrites newer terminal status" was valid. Fixed in 3b113bc.

`resume` checked `terminated` / `pending_approval` against the snapshot it took before the lock, then wrote `status: "idle"` unconditionally — so a terminate committed while the resume waited on the row lock was silently undone.

The locked read now selects `status` as well and re-runs both guards inside the transaction. A concurrent terminate or pending-approval transition makes the resume fail with the same conflict it would have returned had it seen that state up front, and nothing is written.

New test `refuses to resume an agent terminated while the resume was in flight`: a transaction holds the agent row lock, terminates the agent, and commits while the resume is waiting; the resume must reject and the agent must stay `terminated`. It fails without the re-check.

```
npx vitest run server/src/__tests__/agent-instructions-health.test.ts \
  server/src/__tests__/agents-service-clear-error.test.ts
# Test Files  2 passed (2)
# Tests  26 passed (26)

# with the re-check removed
# Tests  1 failed | 22 passed (23)

pnpm --filter @paperclipai/server typecheck   # exit 0
```

For context on the check status: the Greptile check reports failure because this repo requires 5/5 and the last review scored 4/5 — every other check on the head commit is green.

payload.author: dzianisv
payload.body:
P1 "stale update clears newer health" was valid. Fixed in 4924232.

`updateAgent` compared its unlocked `existing.adapterConfig` snapshot against the row it had just written, so with two overlapping updates the later one could read another request's path change as its own correction — deleting health recorded for the path the agent actually uses now, clearing the error and lifting the pause on an agent still running without instructions.

The update transaction now re-reads the pre-update `adapterConfig` with `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` before writing, and compares that. Overlapping updates serialize on the row and each one only reacts to the change it made itself.

New test `does not clear health for the current path when another update lands first`: a transaction holding the row lock commits a path correction plus a failure on the new path while an unrelated rename waits; the rename must preserve the new path's health state and error reason. It fails when the comparison uses the unlocked snapshot.

```
npx vitest run server/src/__tests__/agent-instructions-health.test.ts \
  server/src/__tests__/agents-service-clear-error.test.ts \
  server/src/__tests__/agents-adapter-config-user-secret.test.ts \
  server/src/__tests__/agents-pending-approval-config.test.ts
# Test Files  4 passed (4)
# Tests  33 passed (33)

# with the comparison reverted to the unlocked snapshot
# Tests  1 failed | 23 passed (24)

pnpm --filter @paperclipai/server typecheck   # exit 0
```

That is every P1 from all four review rounds: recovery without a heartbeat, concurrent completions, resume vs. run completion, superseded-path failures, resume vs. terminate, and now overlapping updates. Each has a test that fails without its fix.

payload.author: ericdfields
payload.body:
Thanks — the P1 is valid, and it is now fixed in fa887c410.

You are right about the cause. A configured `hostCallInterceptor` routed **every** `ctx` method through the promise-based fault pipeline, so `ctx.events.on` returned a `Promise` instead of its unsubscribe callback. Plugin cleanup code that calls the returned value would have failed.

The fix restricts the pipeline to `async` methods. I checked every non-`async` method on the harness `ctx`, and they are all genuinely synchronous registration or observation APIs rather than host round trips: `events.on`, the five `register` methods, `streams.open/emit/close`, `logger.*`, `localFolders.declarations`. None of them returns a promise, so none of them loses anything by not being interceptable. They are still recorded in `hostCalls`; they are simply never faulted. I documented that on `TestHarnessOptions.hostCallInterceptor`.

Added a regression test for exactly your case: with an interceptor configured, `ctx.events.on` still returns a callable function synchronously, the interceptor never sees `events.on`, and an async call on the same harness is still intercepted.

Verification after the fix: SDK typecheck clean, 56/56 SDK tests, and the downstream harness consumers still pass — `plugin-llm-wiki` 101/101, `plugin-workspace-diff` 26/26, and the two server `plugin-sdk` suites 13/13.

## CI status update

**Fixed in this push (9f847b0):**

1. **E2E `pipelines-tutorial-flow` → 500 on `ingestCase`** — root cause: `writeCaseEvent` called `logActivity(db as Db, ...)` inside a Postgres transaction. When the activity-log `INSERT` failed (FK violation: `run_id` not yet in `heartbeat_runs` for a fresh fan-out agent run), Postgres put the entire transaction into 'aborted' state. The JS `try/catch` caught the JS error, but subsequent queries (`adjustParentCounts`) then failed with 'current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block'. Fixed with a SAVEPOINT: `SAVEPOINT` before the insert → `RELEASE` on success → `ROLLBACK TO` on failure, restoring the transaction to a clean state.

payload.author: tonio-alucema
payload.body:
All three valid, and the first one I had already convinced myself was handled. It wasn't, and how I got that wrong is the most useful thing here.

**Failed refetches were accepted.** You're right: `isFetchedAfterMount` does not reject a refetch that failed — React Query counts the failed attempt as a fetch after mount while retaining the previous `data`. So after an account switch the retained value is the previous account's list, presented as freshly fetched. `isSuccess` is what actually ties the answer to this session, because a failed refetch flips status to error.

I checked this claim before replying, removed `isFetchedAfterMount`, watched a test fail, and concluded the guard was working. **That test was failing for a different reason** — the inner wizard mounted *during* the fetch and locked its `useState(saved?.x ?? default)` initializers to defaults, so the draft could not appear whatever the gate decided. Fixing the mount gate (below) is what exposed the real behaviour. A fault injection is only evidence if the failure it produces is the one you're claiming.

`isFetchedAfterMount` is now removed rather than kept next to `isSuccess`. It rejects nothing `isSuccess` hasn't already rejected, and no test could distinguish it — which is how a guard rots into decoration.

**Mounting undecided.** Also right, and worse than a discarded restoration: `isLoading` is false whenever retained data exists, so a refetch over a warm cache mounted the wizard while ownership was undecidable, and with the wizard open the persist effect overwrote the customer's *own* draft with defaults before the answer arrived. Now keyed on `isFetching`, which covers refetches. It still releases on failure, so the "Get Started" dead end stays fixed.

**Malformed cleanup.** Fixed — an unreadable draft is judged before the ownership check and doesn't enable the query at all.

Three cases added, and I then re-checked every clause in isolation rather than trusting the suite:

| removed | result |
| --- | --- |
| `isSuccess` | 1 case fails |
| `unauthorized` check | 1 case fails |
| `isFetching` (→ `isLoading`) | 2 cases fail |
| malformed-first ordering | 1 case fails |
| `enabled` narrowing | 1 case fails |

`ui` typecheck clean; full `ui` suite 3963 pass, with only the timezone-dependent `IssueProperties` failure present on `master`.

payload.author: tonio-alucema
payload.body:
### Measured: why this stays on `resetQueries`

#11382 notes that `resetQueries` keeps the query object and can leave `isFetchedAfterMount` false for existing observers, and flags that its own gate depends on that flag. That warning is correct, and it is worth being precise about how far it reaches, since this PR resets the same query key.

I probed both operations against the installed query-core (5.101.4) rather than reasoning about them.

**`removeQueries` does not notify already-subscribed observers.** After the sweep, `getQueryData(["companies"])` returns `undefined` while the mounted observer keeps returning the previous account's data and never refetches. That is the bug this PR exists to fix, so `removeQueries` is not an option here.

**The `isFetchedAfterMount` strand is real, and narrower than it looks.** The baseline the flag compares against is captured when the observer *binds* to the query, so only an observer that binds to an already-warm cache can be rewound below its own baseline:

| Observer | After the sweep |
| --- | --- |
| Binds **warm** (baseline 3), survives the sweep | `isFetchedAfterMount: false` — stranded |
| Same, across two sweeps | `false` — stays stranded |
| Binds **cold** (baseline 0), survives the sweep | `true` |
| Mounts fresh **after** the sweep | `true` |

Two reasons it cannot reach the sign-out sweep:

1. **The sweep unmounts its own victims.** It resets `auth.session` along with everything else, so `CloudAccessGate` (`CloudAccessGate.tsx:113`) renders `<Navigate to="/auth">` on the next render. Every component holding such a gate — `OnboardingWizard`, `AppsConnect.tsx:374`, `InviteLanding` — is inside that tree and unmounts, then remounts fresh on re-entry, which is the last row.
2. **The strand fails closed.** A false `isFetchedAfterMount` makes those gates *withhold* a membership verdict rather than grant one. Even in the single render between reset and redirect, it errs toward refusing — the opposite direction from the leak.

The caveat stays correct where #11382 and the invite-landing change apply it: a *local* reset under an observer that stays mounted. It just does not transfer to a sweep that takes the tree down with it.

The probe was a throwaway and has been deleted; the scenarios are reproducible from the table above with `QueryObserver` plus `setQueryData` to warm the entry before binding.

Both taken, even though they're flagged non-blocking — they're the same failure the widened assertion in this PR was already fixing, one level up.

payload.author: tonio-alucema
payload.body:
Valid. External adapter types are registered into the UI registry only once the adapters query resolves, so until then `listUIAdapters()` returns the built-ins alone and a saved external adapter is indistinguishable from one the deployer disabled. The snap fired on that transient list, replaced the customer's choice with a built-in, and the persist effect wrote it down — so a reload made it permanent.

`useAdapterRegistryLoaded` now gates it. It reads the same query key `useDisabledAdaptersSync` already uses, so it shares that cache entry and adds no request. I added a hook rather than widening that one's return type: it has five production callers and three test mocks, none of which have anything to do with this.

**Worth flagging that this gate fails closed, unlike the ones in #11352 and #11370.** I've been arguing fail-open for the onboarding gates, so the inconsistency is deliberate and the comment explains it: the directions of harm are opposite here. Acting on an unloaded registry silently rewrites a saved answer and persists it. Waiting forever just leaves the selection alone — which is exactly the behaviour that existed before the snap did, so the downside is the status quo. Refusing to change a saved answer is the cheaper mistake.

One case added, confirmed to fail against the code it replaces: a saved external adapter survives a render where the registry has not loaded.

`ui` typecheck clean; 51 pass across the adapter, hook, dialog, config-form and wizard-step suites. I ran the other callers of the hook too, since the module changed.

Attribution note: the substantive commit here is @stubbi's from #9501. The rename and this gate are mine.

payload.author: tonio-alucema
payload.body:
Both valid, both fixed. The first one is destructive, so worth spelling out.

**A failed company query deleted the draft.** React Query reports a failed list as `isLoading === false` with `data` defaulted to `[]`, which is indistinguishable from "settled, and this account owns nothing" — and that is exactly the verdict that wipes the blob. So a customer whose company request timed out lost their in-progress onboarding, permanently, with no way back. An errored list is now treated like a loading one: not decidable, nothing restored, nothing deleted.

Worth noting *why* the fix is "don't mount" rather than "mount with `saved: null` and skip the delete": the persist effect inside the inner component writes the wizard's state back on every change, so mounting with defaults would overwrite the draft within a render or two anyway. There is no mount-but-leave-storage-alone option. Declining to mount is the only thing that actually preserves it, and the comment now says so — that reasoning was implicit before and would not have survived the next edit.

**`localStorage.getItem` was outside the try.** Only the parse was guarded. `getItem` throws outright where a browser denies storage — Safari private mode, a blocked third-party context — and the gate runs during render, so the exception escaped and took the app down. This is a regression against the `loadSavedState()` it replaces, which wrapped the read too. Both are inside the try now.

Two cases added, each confirmed to fail against the code it replaces rather than trusted on a green run: a failed company query leaves the blob intact and mounts nothing, and a throwing `getItem` renders the wizard instead of the exception escaping.

`ui` typecheck clean, 67 pass across the seven onboarding suites.

For context on attribution: the two substantive commits here are @stubbi's from #9900. These two fixes are mine, in the gate their patch introduces — flagging that so the review history reads accurately.

payload.author: tonio-alucema
payload.body:
Valid — `reset()` clears the draft and `handleClose` calls it, so closing the wizard threw on a browser that denies storage.

That is three review rounds finding the same failure at a different call site, which means fixing them one at a time was the wrong shape. `onboardingDraftStorage` now owns the read, the write and the clear, and all four sites go through it. One place can throw; one place handles it.

**Worth recording what went wrong while I did that,** because it is the more useful finding. The bulk edit that introduced the helper also rewrote the body of the helper's own `clear()`, so it called itself — infinite recursion, with its own `catch` swallowing the stack overflow. The draft silently stopped being cleared, and nothing in the new tests noticed. What caught it was `discards a saved draft for a company the signed-in account does not own`, which has been in this branch since @stubbi wrote it and went red immediately.

That is the whole argument for running the suite rather than only the cases you just added — and, separately, for not trusting a mechanical find-and-replace across a file you are also adding a definition to.

One case added, confirmed to fail against the code it replaces: closing the wizard with storage denied calls `closeOnboarding` instead of throwing.

`ui` typecheck clean; full `ui` suite 3922 pass. Two failures, neither related to this branch and both passing in isolation: the timezone-dependent `IssueProperties` case present on `master`, and a timing-based leader-election case in `cross-tab-poll` that only fails under machine load.

payload.author: tonio-alucema
payload.body:
Valid, and finding it corrected reasoning I had asserted in the two commits before this — worth stating plainly.

I claimed declining to mount was the *only* way to protect the draft, because the persist effect would otherwise overwrite it. That is only true when the wizard is **open**: the persist effect is itself gated on `effectiveOnboardingOpen`, so a mounted-but-closed wizard writes nothing. Mounting was never what cost the draft, and I had used that wrong premise to justify the gate.

With it corrected, blocking on an errored list was pure cost. The companies query sets `retry: false`, so the error state sticks — and with no companies the dashboard renders a "Get Started" button wired to `openOnboarding`. A gate returning `null` made that button do **nothing at all**, for as long as the error lasted, which is a worse dead end than the report suggests.

The gate now waits only while the list is *loading*. An error with an empty list stays undecidable for the draft — nothing restored, nothing deleted — but the wizard mounts. Closed, the draft survives untouched for a later load that can verify it; open, the customer is onboarding right now, which supersedes it anyway.

I also renamed `companiesUndecided` to `ownershipUndecidable`, since conflating "can the draft be judged" with "should the wizard mount" is precisely what produced this.

**On the test.** My first version asserted the draft survived an open wizard, which is false for the reason above — it would have encoded the wrong belief as a passing assertion. It now asserts what actually holds in each case, with a second case for the closed wizard where the blob does survive intact. Both confirmed to fail against the code they replace.

`ui` typecheck clean; 69 pass across the six onboarding suites.

payload.author: tonio-alucema
payload.body:
CI caught two things, both interactions with #11371 (the adapter snap, which landed while this was open) and neither visible from either branch alone. Both were green separately.

**The defect is mine.** `useCompany()` types its error as `Error | null`, so I wrote `companiesError !== null`. But `undefined` reaches that line in practice — from any consumer that supplies the company context without an `error` key — and `undefined !== null` is true. So a perfectly healthy company load read as a failure, ownership became undecidable, and the customer's draft was withheld. The question is "is there an error", and only a truthy test asks it.

It surfaced through #11371's adapter test, whose company mock predates this branch and has no `error`. That is not a test artifact — it is exactly the shape of caller that would hit this in production.

**The reverse direction too.** #11371 added `useAdapterRegistryLoaded` to `use-disabled-adapters`, and this branch's test mocks that module. A module mock replaces the *whole* module, so an export the component reaches for and the mock omits is `undefined`, and calling it throws. Every test in the file failed at once, which is the tell.

Worth noting this is the argument for CI testing the merge rather than the branch: I ran the full suite locally on this branch before pushing and it was clean, because the branch didn't have #11371 in it yet. I've since merged `master` in here and reproduced both failures locally before fixing them.

`ui` typecheck clean; full `ui` suite **3952 pass**, with only the timezone-dependent `IssueProperties` failure present on `master`.

payload.author: tonio-alucema
payload.body:
This is the sharpest finding on the branch, and it's right: my own fix two rounds ago reopened the hole this PR exists to close.

**Confirmed the premise before acting.** `useSignOut` invalidates only `auth.session` and `health` — the companies cache is never touched, and `invalidateQueries` keeps serving the old data regardless. So after A signs out and B signs in, a failed companies refetch really does leave A's list in hand. My narrowing ("an error only counts when it left the list empty") then read that non-empty list as authoritative, found A's company id in it, and restored A's onboarding draft for B.

Any error now makes ownership undecidable, whatever the list contains. The mount gate is unchanged — still keyed on loading alone — so the dead end that narrowing was meant to fix stays fixed: the wizard opens, it just doesn't restore, and doesn't delete. The next successful load restores the draft.

Splitting "can the draft be judged" from "should the wizard mount" in an earlier round is what made this a one-line change instead of a re-litigation of both.

**The test for it first passed against the broken code.** I wrote the attack path end to end — A's draft, A's stale companies, B signed in, refetch failed — and it went green before I'd fixed anything, because I saved the draft at step 4, where the agent-name field doesn't render. The assertion couldn't observe a restore either way. It saves at step 3 now and fails as it should. That's the second time on this branch a test asserted on something not rendered; worth naming as a pattern rather than a one-off.

**The underlying cache lifetime is out of scope here and needs its own fix.** This change is defensive and protects onboarding only — any other consumer of `useCompany()` still sees the stale list after a failed post-sign-out refetch. I've filed that separately: sign-out should remove account-scoped cached data rather than invalidating two keys.

`ui` typecheck clean; 73 pass across the seven onboarding suites.

payload.author: nickallevato
payload.body:
Thanks — the `company_skills.forked_from_company_id` finding was correct and is fixed in 36911332b (the commit the latest review reports as last reviewed, so I think the finding carried over from the previous pass).

The preflight no longer excludes `public.companies` as an FK parent. It now excludes only a row's *own* `company_id` column — which says which company owns the row, not which company depends on it — and checks every other column pointing at `companies`, keyed on `pa.id`:

```ts
!(isCompaniesParent(fk) && fk.childColumn === "company_id")
```

```ts
const parentFilter = isCompaniesParent(fk) ? "pa.id = ANY($1)" : "pa.company_id = ANY($1)";
```

On the current schema that covers exactly the two non-`company_id` columns referencing `companies`, both `ON DELETE SET NULL`:

- `company_skills.forked_from_company_id`
- `cli_auth_challenges.requested_company_id`

A surviving company holding either reference now aborts the purge in preflight rather than having the column silently nulled.

payload.author: nickallevato
payload.body:
Closing in favour of the existing server-side work — #6756 fixes the ordering at the source in `companies.remove()` (+3/-2), and #2097 addresses the coverage half. Adding a parallel CLI path on top of those is the wrong shape, and I should have searched the issue and PR list before building this rather than after.

Leaving the findings here so they are not lost:

**1. The ordering fix alone does not close the coverage gap.** 145 tables carry a `company_id`, and plugins create their own `plugin_<slug>_<hash>` schemas with foreign keys into core tables at install time. Any hand-maintained delete list will drift again — that is the pattern behind #2096, #7250, #3038 and #3577, and it is why ten separate issues exist for what looks like one bug. Deriving the table set from `information_schema` rather than a literal list is the part I would still suggest, whether or not it comes from this PR.

**2. Non-`company_id` references to `companies` need handling.** Two columns point at `companies` outside a row's own `company_id`, both `ON DELETE SET NULL`:

- `company_skills.forked_from_company_id`
- `cli_auth_challenges.requested_company_id`

Deleting a company that a *surviving* company forked a skill from silently nulls that provenance rather than failing. Worth a guard in whatever implementation lands. (Credit to the Greptile review on this PR for catching it.)

**3. Unrelated but more impactful: 315 of the schema's 616 foreign keys have no index on the child column.** `heartbeat_runs` alone is referenced by 39 unindexed columns, three of them on `issue_comments`. Because Postgres enforces `ON DELETE CASCADE`/`SET NULL` with a per-row trigger, deleting one parent row scans each unindexed child table once. Measured on a real instance, removing ~11k `heartbeat_runs` rows took over ten minutes; with those indexes present the same work finished in 39 seconds. This slows every cascading delete, not just company removal, and is probably worth its own issue.

For reference, the approach was verified end to end against a live instance — three companies, 833,577 rows across 58 tables, zero orphaned rows across all 616 foreign keys afterwards — so the catalog-derived method does work if anyone wants to pick it up. Happy to open a focused issue for (1) or (2) if that would be useful.
