payload.body:
Both valid, both fixed in c-the-latest commit.

**Auto-open loses company context** — correct, and it defeated the point of the change: opening with empty options started the wizard at the front door with no company, so the new-company path would have created a *second* company instead of giving this one an agent. The dashboard now passes `companyId` and the step, and waits for the goal list before opening so the step is right the first time rather than corrected after.

**Late mission result resets progress** — also correct. The goal query could resolve after the wizard opened, flip `initialStep` from 2 to 3, and the sync effect would move someone off the mission they were typing. Route options are now held back until the mission is known, mirroring how they are already held back while companies load. The step is decided once and never changes underneath an open wizard.

Neither fix adds a request: both read the goal list the launch path already reads, under the query key it already uses.

Worth noting the second one is the same shape as the first — a value that arrives late and moves the UI under the user. Gating on it settling, rather than correcting afterwards, is what removes the class rather than the instance.

payload.author: tonio-alucema
payload.body:
Valid, and it was mine — the previous commit's gate failed **closed**.

Waiting on the goal *data* meant a request that exhausts its retries leaves the value undefined forever, so route onboarding never opens and the dashboard effect returns early every time. An agentless company would have had no automatic onboarding at all, which is worse than the late-step-change this was fixing.

Both gates now wait for the query to **settle** rather than to answer. On failure the mission reads as absent, the customer is asked for it again, and the flow continues. Asking a question twice is recoverable; never opening onboarding is not.

Worth naming, since this is the third finding on this PR and they form a sequence: each fix introduced the next defect one layer over. Empty dialog options → carry the company and step → gate on the data → gate fails closed → gate on settled. The through-line is that every one of them lives in the seam between a value and its consumer, which is exactly where my unit tests don't reach — they all passed at each stage.

This is also the same fail-open rule the wake and provisioning readiness gates already follow: a check guarding a convenience must never be able to block the thing it guards. I had that right elsewhere today and inverted it here.

payload.author: tonio-alucema
payload.body:
Valid — and this is the second finding again, reached through the refetch path rather than the initial load. My fix for the third reopened the hole the second one closed.

**Stopping here rather than patching it.** Four passes, four findings, and the last two trade against each other:

| # | Finding | My fix | What it caused |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | empty dialog options | carry company + step | — |
| 2 | late result moves the wizard | gate on the data arriving | #3 |
| 3 | gate fails closed | gate on the query settling | #4 |
| 4 | late refetch moves the wizard | — | (= #2) |

Patching #4 the obvious way re-creates #3. That is a loop, and it means the defect is structural rather than a sequence of oversights.

**The structural cause.** `initialStep` is a *derived* value feeding an effect that *imperatively* calls `setStep`. Any late change to that value — first load, retry, refetch, cache invalidation — moves a user who is already mid-flow. Gating the input only narrows the window; it cannot close it, because the effect will always re-run when the derived value changes.

**What an actual fix looks like:** decide the step **once**, when the wizard opens, and never again. Concretely, the sync effect should apply `initialStep` on the open transition only, not on every change to it — or the step should be captured into state at open time and the effect should stop depending on it. That is a change to the wizard's step machinery, which is precisely what #9900, #9501 and #8982 are editing, so it needs coordination rather than a quick follow-up commit.

Leaving this open rather than merging. The parts that stand up are worth keeping: `shouldRouteAgentlessCompanyToOnboarding` with its loading and same-path guards, the widened `initialStep` with `ONBOARDING_AGENT_STEP`, the company-level-goal mission signal (`selectDefaultCompanyGoalId` on the existing `queryKeys.goals.list` key — no new fetch), and 29 passing tests. The wiring to the sync effect is the part that needs the structural change above.

Worth noting for whoever continues: every one of these four defects lived in the seam between a value and its consumer, and my unit tests passed at every stage. Tests over the predicates were never going to catch any of them.

payload.author: tonio-alucema
payload.body:
Picked this back up and fixed it structurally, as the last comment said it needed.

**The cause.** `initialStep` is a *derived* value — it comes from the company list and the goal list — feeding an effect that imperatively calls `setStep`. The effect took it as a dependency, so every change to either query moved a customer who was already mid-flow. That is why gating the input never worked: a gate narrows the window, but the effect still re-runs whenever the value changes, so the window never closes. Four passes, and the last two traded against each other, because both were fixing the instance rather than the class.

**The fix.** The step belongs to the *request* that opened the wizard, not to the latest value of the expression that produced it. The effect reads the step through a ref and is keyed on the two things that make a new request: the wizard opening, and the company changing. Navigating from one company's onboarding path to another still re-decides the step; the same request settling on a fresher value does not.

This is the pattern `createdCompanyIdRef` already uses two lines above, with a comment giving the same reason. The file had the answer in it.

**Two simplifications follow.** The route path and the dashboard were each running the same goal query, the same selector and the same settle-gate; that collapses into `useCompanyMission`, with `onboardingStepForCompany` holding the rule that an unknown mission counts as absent. Neither adds a request. And the dashboard now opens onboarding once per company — every input to that effect sat behind a query, so a refetch called `openOnboarding` again and reopened a wizard the customer had closed. That one was live in the previous revision and no review pass caught it.

**On the tests.** The last comment was right that tests over the predicates were never going to catch any of this. `OnboardingWizard.step.test.tsx` renders the real wizard with the real resolver and the real hook, stubbing only the network and the surrounding contexts, and covers all four defects plus the two cases that guard against over-correcting — a different company, and a fresh open, both still re-decide the step. I confirmed each defect case fails against the code it replaces rather than trusting a green run: restoring the old dependency array fails the two "does not move" cases, and restoring the data gate fails the two fail-open cases.

3909 pass in the full `ui` suite. The one remaining failure is in `IssueProperties.test.tsx`, is timezone-dependent, and reproduces on this branch with these changes removed.

#9900, #9501 and #8982 still touch this file and are all 3-4 weeks stale. I did not wait on them. The change to the step machinery is four lines, so a rebase is cheap either way.

payload.author: tonio-alucema
payload.body:
Valid, and unlike the previous four this one is not another turn of the same loop — it is in the step this change routes people *to*, rather than in how that step is chosen. Fixed, along with a worse one next to it.

**The mission was discarded.** `handleConfirmMission` advanced without writing anything when the company already existed. That branch was dead code until now: a company reached step 2 only by creating itself on step 1, one line below, which writes the goal on the way through. The dashboard now opens an agentless company directly on that step, so the customer types a mission, presses "Confirm mission", and lands on the agent step with the company holding none — the exact state this PR exists to remove. Downstream only makes it quieter: `handleLaunchToDashboard` falls back to `selectDefaultCompanyGoalId`, finds nothing, and links the onboarding project to no goal. It now creates the company-level goal, guarded on `createdCompanyGoalId` so going back and confirming again does not add a second.

**And the step could not be completed at all.** Checking the same branch turned up the harder failure: `companyName` is only ever typed on step 1, so a company entering the wizard further along has none. Step 2 prints the name in its own copy, and *both* ways forward — the button and the Enter key — are gated on `companyName.trim()`. A customer sent there was stuck on a step asking about a company it could not name. It is now backfilled from the company list, beside the effect that already backfills the issue prefix for the same company and the same reason.

**Scope.** Both predate this branch and are unchanged on `master`. Neither was reachable there. This PR is what makes the mission step the default destination for an agentless company, so they are this PR's to fix.

Three cases added to the seam suite: the step names its company and can be completed, confirming writes the goal, confirming twice writes one. Each confirmed to fail against the code it replaces — removing the name backfill fails all three, restoring the bare `setStep(3)` fails the two about writing.

3912 pass in the full `ui` suite; the one failure is the timezone-dependent `IssueProperties` case that reproduces on this branch with these changes removed.

payload.author: tonio-alucema
payload.body:
Both valid, both mine, both fixed.

**Company switch retains onboarding state (P1).** Correct, and my previous commit is what sharpened it. That branch replaced the company id and prefix and kept everything else — which was survivable while `createdCompanyGoalId` could only be set by creating a company on step 1. Making the existing-company path set it too means a customer who confirms a mission for one company and then opens another hits the guard that stops a second goal, reading the *first* company's id: the second company's mission is silently skipped, and the launch path links its project to the first company's goal. The branch now clears the name, the mission text and the created resource ids alongside the id it was already clearing. It runs exactly where it already ran — only when the route introduces a company that is not the one in hand — so a route that merely names the company the wizard created still claims nothing.

**Enter has no in-flight guard.** Also correct. Every button in the wizard is disabled on `loading`; the keyboard path was not, so a second Enter re-enters a handler whose guard is state the first has not set yet. On the new mission path that is two goals for one mission. Worth noting it was already two companies for one company on step 1 and two agents for one hire on step 4 — same shape, older. One check at the top of `handleKeyDown` covers all of them rather than three guards in three handlers.

Two cases added, both confirmed to fail against the code they replace: a mission is not carried across a company switch, and a second Enter writes one goal.

Separately, the full-suite run surfaced an order-dependent failure in the new mission-hook suite — a single macrotask tick was enough in isolation but not under load. Both new suites now drain until the value settles instead of guessing at a tick count. 3914 pass over two consecutive full runs, with the same timezone-dependent `IssueProperties` failure the base has.

On the pattern: these last two are the same class as the original four — state that outlives the thing it describes. Worth saying plainly that the previous commit created the first one rather than merely exposing it.

payload.author: tonio-alucema
payload.body:
Both valid. Fixed.

**Failed lookup duplicates missions.** Correct, and it is the bill for failing open — worth paying properly rather than reversing the decision. `useCompanyMission` reports a failed lookup as "no mission", so a company that has one gets asked again; writing unconditionally then left two active company-level goals. One correction to the finding: within the session the launch path uses `createdCompanyGoalId`, so the project does link to the new goal — but everywhere *outside* this wizard `selectDefaultCompanyGoalId` picks the earlier one, so the mission the customer just typed loses anyway. Same outcome, different route.

`handleConfirmMission` now reads the goal list once before writing and updates the existing goal rather than adding another. Adopting the old goal and discarding what they typed would be the other way out, and it is wrong: they answered the question on a step that asked it, so their answer is the mission. A read that fails still writes — an unwritten mission stays the worse error at every level.

This does add one request, on the mission path only, at the moment the customer presses "Confirm mission". The step *decision* still adds none.

**Company dismissal history is lost.** Also correct, and worse than reported: the ref died with the component too, so navigating off the dashboard and back re-offered as well — not just switching companies. `claimOnboardingOffer` now holds the set, at module scope, so an offer stays declined for the visit. A reload offers again, which I think is the right scope: a reload is a new visit, not the same one continuing. Happy to make it durable if you disagree, but that is a product call about how insistent onboarding should be, so I did not make it unilaterally here.

Five cases added, each confirmed to fail against the code it replaces: the mission is updated rather than duplicated, a failed pre-write read still writes, and each company is offered once in any order.

3919 pass over two consecutive full runs. The one failure is the timezone-dependent `IssueProperties` case that reproduces on this branch with these changes removed.

Separately — the `General tests (workspaces-b)` failure on the previous run is `@paperclipai/adapter-utils > execution-target-sandbox.test.ts`, an empty stdout from a subprocess launch. This branch touches only `ui/src/**`, and that lane passed on the two commits before it. Flake, not a regression. `verify` failed only as its aggregate.

payload.author: tonio-alucema
payload.body:
Valid. Fixed — and it is the last open instance of the class the previous rounds have been working through: state that outlives the thing it describes.

The company-switch reset clears the created resource ids, but a write already in flight still holds the old company in its closure. When it lands it writes into the state the reset just cleared, so the new company inherits the old company's goal — and the guard that stops a second mission then reads that as "already written" and skips asking. The reset existed to prevent exactly that, so the write was undoing it.

Both writes now compare the company they started for against `createdCompanyIdRef`, which every render keeps current, and return instead of writing when the wizard has moved on. The server work is done and correct either way; only the attribution is declined. The `invalidateQueries` calls moved above the guard — the cache for the company that *was* written should refresh whether or not this wizard still cares about it. I gave the agent write next door the same guard, since this change routes people to that step too.

One case added, confirmed to fail against the code it replaces: switching companies while a mission write is in flight leaves the second company on the mission step, and it writes its own mission.

**On the two red CI lanes, neither of which is this branch.** `Verify serialized server suites (5/5)` is `@paperclipai/server > issue-closed-workspace-routes.test.ts`, failing with `transient database error`, `revalidation read failed` and a 5s timeout. The earlier `General tests (workspaces-b)` was `adapter-utils > execution-target-sandbox.test.ts` returning empty stdout from a subprocess. This branch touches only `ui/src/**`; both lanes passed on earlier commits of this same branch; `verify` fails only as the aggregate of its lanes.

**And a caveat on my own numbers.** My machine is currently at load 15, and full local suite runs have gone noisy — different unrelated files fail each run (`AgentConfigForm`, `TestPanel`, `AuditFeed`, `TweakPanel`, `Projects`, `ScheduleEditor`, `RunWorkspaceRecoverySurface`), all pass in isolation, and none import anything this branch touches. The reliable local figure is from the previous commit under a quiet machine: two consecutive runs at 3919 pass, with only the timezone-dependent `IssueProperties` failure that reproduces with these changes removed. CI is the better authority for the full suite here, so I would rather flag that than quote a number I do not trust.

payload.author: tonio-alucema
payload.body:
Valid, and the right response is to stop adding this check one site at a time — adding a third and fourth copy would be exactly the shape of mistake this branch is named for.

`stillTheSameCompany` now holds the rule once, with the reason, and all five writes ask it: the mission write, the agent write, and the goal, project and issue writes in the launch path. It never cancels the server work, which is done and correct either way. It declines only to record that work against a company it does not belong to.

The company *creation* path asks the same question from the other end. Nothing was in hand when it started, so "unchanged" means still nothing. A route that supplied a company while the request was open has taken over the wizard, and adopting the company just created would fight it — and would leave the customer on a company they never navigated to.

The `invalidateQueries` calls moved above every guard: the company that *was* written should have its cache refreshed regardless of where this wizard has got to.

**One note on the test, because it is the more useful finding.** The case I wrote for the creation path passed against the unguarded code on the first attempt. It asserted on the rendered company name, which reads "Acme" either way — the switch reset clears the name and the backfill refills it from a company list that has no entry for the company just created. A test that cannot fail is worse than no test, because it reads as coverage. It now asserts on the global company selection, which only happens when the created company is adopted, and it does fail against the unguarded code.

That is the same error class as the original four, one level up: an observable that is true for the wrong reason. Fault-injecting every case is what caught it, and it is why I have been doing that rather than trusting a green run.

**On CI:** both lanes that were red earlier are green on the last run — `General tests (workspaces-b)` and `Verify serialized server suites (5/5)` — which confirms those were flakes rather than this branch. My local full-suite runs remain noisy under machine load; the rotating failures all pass in isolation and none import anything this branch touches, so I am treating CI as the authority on the full suite.

payload.author: tonio-alucema
payload.body:
Both valid. The first is a regression my previous commit introduced, not an older defect, and it is worth naming as such.

**Stale completions.** I put the ownership check in the wrong place in the hire path — before the CEO instruction seeding. A company switch mid-hire therefore left a *hired agent with adapter defaults and no instructions file*. That inverts the rule the check exists for: the server work is done and belongs to whoever it was done for; only the attribution is this wizard's to decline. The seeding now runs first, and the check guards `setCreatedAgentId` and the step change after it.

The launch path had the matching gap at its end. The goal, project and issue writes were guarded, but the finish — select the company, `reset()`, navigate — was not. A switch mid-launch would take the customer back to the company they had left and `reset()` would discard the progress they had started on the new one. Guarded now, after all the server work completes.

**Route-company withdrawal.** Correct, and it is a half-fix of mine: I made the *replacement* branch clear the company-scoped state and left the *withdrawal* branch clearing only the id and prefix. Those are the same event — this company is no longer the wizard's — and clearing half of it leaves a goal id that the next company reads as "mission already written", so it never gets asked. `clearCompanyScopedState` now holds that list once and both branches call it.

One case added, confirmed to fail against the code it replaces: a mission confirmed on a company's onboarding path is not carried through a navigation to the unprefixed route.

Worth stating the shape, because two rounds in a row have now been my own fixes rather than pre-existing code: guarding *entry* to async work is wrong, guarding *attribution* after it is right, and any state that describes one company must be cleared on every path where the wizard stops holding that company — not on the first one I happened to find.

57 pass across the route, hook, offer and wizard suites. Not quoting a full-suite number this time: this machine is at load 28 and the figure would not mean anything. CI has run the suite green on the last two commits.

payload.author: tonio-alucema
payload.body:
Valid on the retention, wrong on the mechanism — and writing the test for it found a race I introduced two commits ago.

**The retention is real.** The route recorded ownership only when it named a company the wizard was not already holding, so a company the wizard *created* was never route-owned and never withdrawn. Create on step 1, visit that company's own onboarding path, then go to `/onboarding`: the wizard shows "create a company" while still holding the previous one, and the next confirmation writes the customer's new mission into it. That is precisely the failure the withdrawal branch was written to prevent, reached by a path it could not see. Ownership is now recorded whenever the route names a company, including the one in hand; only the clearing stays conditional.

That reverses a rule the code documented — not recording ownership there was protecting wizard-created work from a later `/onboarding`. The trade is deliberate: `/onboarding` is a request to start a company, so honouring it and losing step-1 progress beats silently writing into a different company. Flagging it explicitly in case you read that trade the other way.

**The mechanism in the report is wrong.** It describes the create path running and its adoption being rejected, leaving an orphan company and a stuck wizard. That cannot happen — `handleConfirmMission` branches on `createdCompanyId`, so a held company takes the existing-company branch and the create path is unreachable. No company is created and nothing is stuck. The consequence is a mission written to the wrong company, which is bad for a different reason.

**The race the test found.** The create path sets `createdCompanyId` and then asks `stillTheSameCompany(company.id)` before writing the goal — but the ref that answers is a render mirror, and the render had not always happened by then. So the handler that had just created the company could be told it no longer owned it, skip the goal write, and leave the customer sitting on the mission step they had just completed. Network latency usually hides it, which is the worst property a bug can have. The mirror is now updated eagerly beside the state, the way the route ref already was.

That one is worth naming: the guard I added to prevent stale writes could itself reject a *fresh* one. I only found it because the new case drove the real step-1 flow rather than asserting on the guard in isolation.

Two cases added, each confirmed to fail against the code it replaces.

Load on my machine finally dropped, so the full local suite is meaningful again: **3923 pass**, with only the timezone-dependent `IssueProperties` failure that reproduces with these changes removed.

payload.author: tonio-alucema
payload.body:
Valid, again - the ownership tracking I added claimed too much.

The ref was set whenever the route *named* a company, including one the wizard created itself. Create a company in the wizard, navigate to that company's onboarding path, then on to `/onboarding`, and the company is cleared: the route claimed something it never supplied.

payload.author: nickallevato
payload.body:
Follow-up: I can now show exactly why the package stylesheet wins, instead of describing it as a possibility.

`ui/src/main.tsx` imports the package stylesheet before `index.css`, so the source order is correct. The build then splits the CSS into two chunks, and `ui/dist/index.html` links them in the opposite order:

```html
<link href="/assets/index-<hash>.css">   <!-- our index.css: .paperclip-mdxeditor -->
<link href="/assets/main-<hash>.css">    <!-- @mdxeditor/editor: ._editorRoot_… -->
```

The package's chunk is the second link, so it is later in the cascade. Both selectors are specificity 0,1,0 and both apply to the same element, so the later one wins and `--baseTextContrast` resolves to the package's light-palette `var(--slate-12)`.

Verified against a local production build:

- `.paperclip-mdxeditor{` at byte 367281 of `assets/index-<hash>.css`
- `_editorRoot_1e2ox_53{--accentBase` at byte 11353 of `assets/main-<hash>.css`
- `index.html` links `index-<hash>.css` first and `main-<hash>.css` second

This is why the fix targets specificity and not import order. Import order in `main.tsx` is already correct and does not survive chunk splitting.

payload.author: nickyleach
payload.body:
Follow-up on the concurrency review of the unsigned ask-first request handling. Fixed in ef1d0c00e.

The gateway creates an ask-first request in two steps: it inserts the row with a null signature, then it signs the row and sets the expiry. A concurrent matching call could observe the row in this window, treat the null signature as an abandoned create, and expire it. The first call then signed the expired row and returned approval_required with an unapprovable action request id, while the concurrent call created a duplicate pending request.

Changes:

- Distinguish an abandoned row from a live in-flight row by createdAt age. Treat an unsigned row as abandoned only after a two-minute grace time. Before that, the concurrent call replays the live request, so it does not duplicate or expire the row.
- Guard the sign update with the pending status so it never resurrects an expired row. When the row is already resolved, throw a retriable conflict instead of an unapprovable approval card.

Tests: a recent unsigned request is now replayed, not expired, and no duplicate is created; a genuinely old unsigned request is still expired so a retry gets a fresh, signable request. All tool-gateway tests pass.

Thanks — good catch on the startup window. Fixed in 0d1f8b0.

**The window:** because the loader is backfilled onto the shared lifecycle asynchronously (`setLoader` in the `.finally` of `bundledPluginsStartup`), `server.listen()` could accept requests before that ran on deployments that don't otherwise gate boot on plugin readiness — self-hosted, or managed instances with no declared sandbox environments (`applyManagedEnvironments` returns early before `await opts.pluginsReady` in those cases). During that window a route-driven `enable/disable/unload` drove a loader-less lifecycle: `activateReadyPlugin` no-ops (no runtime services), so the plugin persists `ready` and the dispatcher registers its tools, but no worker is spawned.

**The fix:** `index.ts` now `await`s the settled `bundledPluginsStartup` promise immediately before `server.listen()`, alongside the existing external-adapter wait. No request can reach a plugin route until `setLoader` has run.

**Why this ordering is safe:** managed instances that declare sandbox environments already blocked `listen()` on this same promise via `applyManagedEnvironments`, and they boot fine — so plugin workers do not require the HTTP server to be listening during activation. The promise never rejects (createApp swallows and logs bundled-plugin failures), so a degraded plugin cannot block the listener. The change adds no new activation path, so there is no double-start risk.

PR description also updated with the full required template sections.

payload.author: jetooh
payload.body:
CI note: the red jobs here come from `master`, not from this branch.

Every failing job stops at `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` with:

```
ERR_PNPM_LOCKFILE_CONFIG_MISMATCH  Cannot proceed with the frozen installation.
The current "overrides" configuration doesn't match the value found in the lockfile
```

Cause: commit eb6c6a8 (#10724) set `lexical: 0.49.0` in the lockfile `overrides` block and in `ui/package.json`, but the root `package.json` still pins `pnpm.overrides.lexical` to `0.46.0`.

- At `3cd5967`, the parent commit, the lockfile `overrides` said `lexical: 0.46.0` and matched the root manifest.
- At `eb6c6a8` and later, they differ.

This branch changes no `package.json`, no `pnpm-lock.yaml` and no patches, so the policy job does not regenerate a lockfile and every downstream job installs from the mismatched pair.

`pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` exits 0 on this branch at its base commit `88e1ccb`, which is before `eb6c6a8`.

#11328 ("chore(lockfile): refresh pnpm-lock.yaml") looks like the fix already in flight. I am happy to rebase once it lands, or to align the root override in this PR if you prefer — say which you want.

The `review`, `policy`, `security-review`, Socket and Snyk checks are green.

payload.body:
## Round 6 — indirect shell expansion bypass fixed (`bcd14c204`)

Addresses the open P1 from the [10:40Z review](https://github.com/paperclipai/paperclip/pull/11325#discussion_r0): **"Indirect shell expansion bypasses gates"**.

### The finding was valid

The hook receives the `PreToolUse` command *before* bash expands it. So `g=gh; $g pr merge 460` contains no literal `gh pr merge` substring — the extractor returned empty and the script fell through to the empty-result `allow`, while bash then expanded `$g` and merged with **none** of the three gates evaluated.

Confirmed empirically against the generated script at the previous SHA (`33b795e78`):

```
PRE-FIX:  g=gh; $g pr merge 460 --squash  => ALLOW   <-- bypass
POST-FIX: g=gh; $g pr merge 460 --squash  => DENY
```

### Fix

Both implementations (TS parser + generated bash extractor, kept symmetric) now treat a `pr merge` token pair whose **command word is a shell expansion** as an unauditable target and deny the whole command via the existing `__unresolvable_merge__` sentinel:

- `$var pr merge N` · `${VAR} pr merge N` · `$(...) pr merge N` · `` `...` pr merge N ``

Requiring the expansion marker (rather than denying any bare `pr merge`) avoids over-blocking ordinary tool calls — `git commit -m "pr merge fix"` stays allowed. The deny reason now names the indirect case so the agent knows to re-issue a literal `gh pr merge <PR>`.

### Verification

Driving the **real generated bash** with a stubbed `curl`:

| Command | Verdict |
|---|---|
| `g=gh; $g pr merge 460 --squash` | DENY |
| `${GH} pr merge 460` | DENY |
| `$(which gh) pr merge 460` | DENY |
| `` `which gh` pr merge 460 `` | DENY |
| `git commit -m "pr merge fix"` | ALLOW |
| `gh pr view 460` | ALLOW |
| `gh pr merge 460 --squash` (gates pass) | ALLOW |

- **53/53 tests pass** (was 49) — 4 exploit variants + 2 false-positive guards, both at parser level and end-to-end through the generated script.
- `tsc --noEmit` clean · `check-no-git-push.mjs` clean · `bash -n` clean.

### Note on the 10:33Z "tab whitespace" P1

That one is **stale** — it was posted at 10:33Z against the state before `33b795e78` (10:37Z), which already widened the match to `gh[[:space:]]+pr[[:space:]]+merge`. Regression tests for tabs between every token pair are in the suite and green.

Thanks — both findings were valid and are fixed in e0b281d.

**Issue 2 — credentials cross adapter boundaries.** Agreed, and this was the more serious of the two. The route now requires the agent's adapter type to match the requested type, not just the company:

if (
  discoveryAgent

```
